title: Search and Increasing Returns, or, No One Makes You Push to Github
raw_summary: Attention conservation notice : An economistic argument that computer networks are nigh-doomed to effective centralization, by someone who is neither an economist nor a computer scientist. Arcane, speculative, and not actionable even if correct. You would be better off spending your time reading a book . Drafted in 2018, and deliberately not much updated. Posted now because I found myself re-using the joke of the subtitle in an e-mail. Twitter is awful for many reasons , but not the least of them is the way it makes its users feel forced to keep using it. ( One such complaint among many .) Early visions of how it could contribute to a beneficient or at least harmless ecosystem, such Steven Berlin Johnson's (*), presumed that it would be much less sticky , a more old-fashioned website people could leave. Now, more recently Johnson has written a spectacularly wrong-headed piece hailing blockchain as a blow for re-decentralizing the Web. Of course, the primary working example of a block chain is Bitcoin, which is heavily centralized in holdings, in processing power, and in exchanges. And there are economies-of-scale reasons to expect this would be true of anything using either proof of work or proof of stake. But suppose the problem with Bitcoin is just that it's not got a very compelling use: imagine if keeping your car idling 24/7 produced solved Sudokus you could trade for heroin --- @Theophite, 16 August 2018 and that nobody has a use for blockchains , not really. Git repositories, on the other hand, are the part of the blockchain idea that's actually good for something: a way of tracking changes, with many authors, where it is very, very hard to go back and alter history without being caught. And git repositories are things that are in-principle easy to copy and move around, and could be hosted on any machine running HTTP (or, heck, FTP). So why does Github exist , let alone hold the position it does? The answer, I think, comes in two parts. The first is that focal points are subject to increasing returns via network effects. The second is that search engines create and/or amplify focal points . Put these two together, and you get a very strong tendency for any particular line of activity --- be it trading solved sudokus for heroin or open-source software development --- to concentrate in just one, or at most a few, online locations. Incidentally: This doesn't necessarily lock in first-mover advantage, because other forces can overcome this (revulsion, technical superiority), but it does mean that it will be very hard to avoid having at most a few dominant locations at any one time. It also means that the transitions between dominant locations will be brief . If we really wanted to re-decentralize, we'd have to (1) get rid of focal points, or (2) get rid of search engines as we've known them, or (3) somehow make search conduct users to a distributed, decentralized focal "non-point" (focal blob? focal rhizome?). I therefore strongly suspect we are not going to re-decentralize. But then I didn't expect the Web would centralize as much as it has, despite having literally learned my Brian Arthur and Paul David at my father's knee, so what do I know? *: To be clear, I have been a fan of Johnson's books since Interface Culture and Emergence . I am picking on two of his essays, but that's because I think he is too ready to find encouraging signs for a certain vision of how the Internet could transform the world for the better. To be clear, I share the vision, but now hold out little hope for it . (Tweakage, 2 June 2026: Small changes in the last paragraph, avoid re-using the word "point" so much.) title: Using Kedro to build reusable reflection systems for enterprise AI agents
raw_summary: Modular pipelines, data contracts, and approval gates for agent improvement In a recent post on this channel, “ Smart contracts for AI agents ”, we described embedding governance directly into each agent through a machine-readable manifest and a runtime sidecar proxy. We noted how it addresses four scaling problems: framework-selection paralysis, compliance drift, reactive validation, and vendor lock-in. The smart contract defines what the agent is, and the sidecar enforces it. However, an agent may operate fully within its declared boundaries while still producing weak outputs, for example, by falling short of quality targets, or drifting in patterns that emerge only across dozens of runs and several campaigns. The smart contracts approach can tell you that your agent used an unapproved model or accessed restricted data, but it cannot tell you about the quality of the emails your sales agent writes on your behalf. Are they any good? Are they improving over time? What is missing is a way to accumulate learning at scale. That requires another layer, positioned above enforcement, which converts production traces into organizational knowledge. This article describes what a learning layer looks like and how to build it as shared infrastructure rather than a one-off feature bolted onto each agent. Why learning gets trapped in silos Enterprises running multiple agents tend to converge on the same organizational problem. One team builds an evaluation rubric for a sales outreach agent. Another adds observability to a marketing campaign agent. A third writes its own reflection workflow for customer care. Each team reinvents the same cycle: generate output → score it → detect what went wrong → propose a fix → review and approve it → apply it. Their fixes stay local to their agents. A regression test written for the B2B sales agent never reaches the consumer marketing agent. A quality pattern that recurs in both sales and marketing sits in two separate dashboards. There isn’t a portfolio-level view of which agents are improving, which are degrading, and what failure modes they share. The underlying issue is that improvement is treated as a feature of individual agents, not as a common layer that every team and campaign can reuse. This builds on an idea we introduced in our original article, “ Agentic AI Mesh ”, which described feedback loops where “agents configured to critique outputs of other agents… can be used to signal positive and negative performance, triggering the automated development of configuration variations that can be tested and scored.” What that article didn’t specify was the shared infrastructure, such as approval gates, versioning, and cross-campaign visibility, that is needed to operationalize that loop, and that is what we cover here. A shared reflection infrastructure Agentic reflection is the process by which a system designed to evaluate agent performance reviews an agent’s outputs against predefined quality criteria, identifies errors or reasoning gaps, and proposes improvements. The learning part happens when improvements are approved, captured, and reused so that mistakes are not repeated. Building this as shared infrastructure requires the same three structural properties that make the smart contract architecture work. Declarative: Evaluation logic, reflection prompts, approval rules, and improvement steps are written down and versioned rather than embedded in ad hoc scripts that only the team that wrote them can access. Modular: Generation, evaluation, signal detection, reflection, and application are separate stages that can change independently. A team that wants to swap the evaluation model does not need to touch the generation pipeline. Reusable: The loop, the deterministic checks, and the audit trail are common to every agent, and the scouts flag when the same type of failure recurs in more than one agent. Approved changes are versioned and visible across the portfolio, so a fix found by one team can be reviewed and adopted by another. A worked example using Kedro We built an example of this approach using Kedro , an open-source Python framework, which offers a modular pipeline structure and explicit data contracts to provide a set of building blocks. Using Kedro to take care of the surrounding orchestration enabled us to focus on the reflection and learning workflow. To show how this pattern works in practice, we built an example that applies the same reflection and learning workflow across three business functions (B2B sales, consumer marketing, and customer care) in a telecommunications company. The improvement lifecycle Each function uses different data sources, prompts, and evaluation criteria. The improvement lifecycle is identical for all three: Generate: run the AI workflow and capture outputs. Evaluate: score outputs against quality criteria using a versioned rubric and an LLM judge. Identify signals and patterns: detect recurring issues across runs, such as tone drift, hallucinations, missing required content, or score regressions. Reflect: generate targeted recommendations such as prompt updates, skill edits, or evaluation logic changes. Review and approve: a human reviewer inspects the proposed changes and approves or rejects them through an explicit approval gate. Nothing goes live without it. Apply: version and commit the approved changes, and record each one in an audit log. A screen from the Kedro reflection agent example In the example, the generate, evaluate, detect, reflect, and apply stages are separate pipelines, with review and approval acting as an approval gate. The pipelines, deterministic checks, and approval gate are shared, while the prompts, style guides, rubrics, and LLM judge dimensions change by use case. Reflection also proposes new regression cases derived from the failures it found. Once approved, they are committed to that agent’s evaluation dataset (alongside any approved changes to the prompt, skills, or other configurable components) then every change is recorded in a single audit log. The signal moves between agents. When the same type of failure recurs in more than one agent, the scouts record it in a shared signal index and flag it as a cross-unit pattern, rather than leaving it as two unrelated findings in two isolated dashboards. A reviewer can then decide whether a fix belongs to one agent or should be adopted by others. Reflection maps onto a Shape-Control-Operate (SCO) lifecycle. Prompts and evaluation criteria are defined in the Shape phase, and evaluation scoring runs in the Control phase. The evidence gathered while agents Operate then feeds approved changes back into the Shape-phase artifacts, which closes the loop. How the evaluation step works Evaluation uses a fixed set of benchmark cases but does not rely on a single correct or “golden” output. Each case, stored in Langfuse and cached locally, pairs a scenario — customer, product, and case ID — with a rubric defining required and forbidden content, expected call to action, tone, and other agent-specific criteria. For each case, the generation pipeline produces an output, which is then scored in two ways: Deterministic checks validate objective requirements such as subject presence, body length, CTA presence, and fabricated SKU-like tokens. An LLM judge evaluates qualitative dimensions such as writing quality, personalization, and groundedness. These dimensions can vary by agent (for example, empathy or compliance). A case passes when the average score across all scorers meets the configured threshold. Results are captured at both case and aggregate levels and logged to Langfuse, enabling teams to compare runs after prompt changes, inspect traces, and feed the findings back into the reflection loop. title: Building production-ready GraphRAG systems with Kedro
raw_summary: A demo project to manage the graph, vector index, and relational store Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) works well for factual lookup. For example, if you use semantic similarity to retrieve a document, you’ll usually find the correct passage. However, it struggles when the lookup requires reasoning across relationships, say if the answer depends on facts that are distributed across records that share little lexical or semantic similarity with each other. As an illustration for healthcare, a search might want to discover the risk of a particular medication to patients with a certain condition. A typical query might be: “ For a chronic kidney disease patient, which medication may not be safe and interact with their poor kidney function? ” A dense retriever might return the passages whose embeddings sit the closest to the query vector, like a chunk about chronic kidney disease and another about drugs with contraindications for renal patients. But to respond to this question as accurately as possible, we’d have to gather information from separate records, like a diagnosis note, a lab report, or a drug prescription. None of these directly references the others, and there is no structure that encodes the intersection of all of these pieces of data. GraphRAG addresses this by pairing semantic search with a knowledge graph that represents the structure explicitly: entities such as conditions, medications, and test results become nodes, and the relationships between them become edges. Before passing context to the language model, the system traverses the relationships connected to the retrieved entities so the model can reason across linked nodes rather than treating each document in isolation. In this article, we describe how we used Kedro to build a demo of a simple reference implementation. The basics In our example, the GraphRAG system maintains three representations of the same underlying data, which need to stay consistent with each other as source data changes. The representations are: a knowledge graph for relationship traversal a vector index for semantic retrieval a relational store for aggregate statistics. Data engineering matters as much as retrieval because of the need for consistency. Inconsistent data arises, for example, when data teams use a collection of scripts, run in undocumented order, with no guarantee that the graph, the vector index, and the analytics store are produced from the same source run. When the knowledge graph becomes stale relative to the embeddings, the retrieval and graph traversal return contradictory context. As a result, the model resolves the inconsistency silently, and may resolve it incorrectly. A data engineering pipeline feeds all three data stores. Incremental updates compound the challenge. Rebuilding the full graph each time new records arrive is impractical at production scale. A production system needs targeted, merge-capable updates that leave unchanged nodes and edges untouched while incorporating new information: a classic data engineering pipeline problem. An example pipeline Using Kedro , we built a five-stage pipeline demo over a synthetic healthcare dataset of 55,500 patient records covering conditions, medications, insurers, admission types, diagnostic results, and demographics. The full source is on the Kedro Academy GitHub repository . While this example is based on healthcare data, none of this structure is specific to healthcare, and the example is deliberately simple to keep it self-contained and easy to run. The entity extraction, graph building patterns, and incremental merge logic apply to any domain with typed entities and relationships. A graph built from a synthetic healthcare dataset of 55,500 patient records in this simple and self-contained example. The pipeline stages are as follows: Clean and summarize: The first stage normalizes raw records, removes duplicates, and computes summary statistics per entity. We used patient counts per condition, average billing amounts per admission type, and result distributions across demographic groups. This stage stores them in SQLite and reuses them as retrieval context in later stages. Build the knowledge graph: The second stage extracts entities and typed relationships. Nodes represent conditions , medications , insurers , admission types , test results , and blood types . Edges carry a relationship label (TREATED_WITH, COVERED_BY, ADMITTED_AS, SHOWS_RESULT, ASSOCIATED_WITH) and a weight recording how frequently each relationship appears in the data. The stage produces a NetworkX JSON graph with 30 nodes and 120 weighted edges, and an interactive D3.js visualization of the entity network. Incrementally update the graph: Rather than rebuilding from scratch on each data refresh, the next stage merges new records into the existing graph using create-or-update semantics. It adds new entities, increments edge weights for existing relationships, and leaves unchanged portions untouched. In this demo, each run of the stage merges a fixed batch of 5,000 records rather than the full corpus, and it updates only the knowledge graph. We designed it to model a real production constraint: while rebuilding a relatively small graph like this is cheap and resolves in a few seconds, a production-sized knowledge graph based on a larger, more complex set of data would take much longer. Generate vector embeddings: For each entity, the next stage generates a natural-language summary of its characteristics and connections, then embeds those summaries using OpenAI’s text-embedding-3-small model . This stage stores the embeddings in ChromaDB for semantic similarity search at query time. Answer questions: The final stage runs an AI agent backed by GPT-4o. When a query arrives, the agent embeds it and queries ChromaDB for the most similar entity summaries. Starting from those results, it traverses one hop across the knowledge graph to collect neighboring entities and the relationships between them. That combined context (semantic matches plus explicit graph structure) goes to the model. Standard RAG asks, “ What is most similar to this query? ” This stage adds, “ What else is connected to those results? ” This is a hybrid GraphRAG pattern: vector retrieval followed by graph traversal. All five stages write to three different backends, and Kedro’s Data Catalog manages loading and saving for all of them from a single configuration file. Every dataset (the NetworkX graph, the ChromaDB collection, the SQLite statistics table, the LangChain prompt template) is declared in catalog.yml so there is one place to see where each input and output lives and there are no separate scripts to reconcile manually. A full default run builds all three stores from the same source data. The incremental update refreshes only the knowledge graph; keeping the vector index and statistics in step with it would require extending their pipelines in the same way. Each stage is an independent Kedro pipeline with explicit inputs and outputs. The graph construction logic, the embedding model, and the retrieval strategy sit in separate modules. Swapping the embedding model requires changing one node and its catalog entry, while the graph and statistics stages are unaffected. Kedro-Viz renders the full data lineage across all five stages, and a published Kedro-Viz build can be viewed without any installation on the viewer’s side. This approach also means it is possible to treat generative AI components as first-class Data Catalog entries, rather than scripts or loose objects spread around the project. It makes them easier to manage and keep track of, and they can be used as input or output for nodes like any other entry. Through the use of Kedro, generative AI datasets receive easy credentials management and follow the same load/save contract as other Kedro datasets. The graph_update pipeline is excluded from the default run and must be invoked explicitly. It writes to the same catalog entry …

title: What changes when your design system can talk to an AI?
raw_summary: Rebuilding a UI with QuantumBlack Design System, Claude Code, and the Figma MCP In our recent blog post, “ When everyone can build, design is the differentiator ”, we introduced QuantumBlack Design System (QBDS). We made the argument that an AI-native design system is more than a component library and its purpose is as an infrastructure that lets agentic developers make fewer guesses. The article described the system and our philosophy. Over the past few weeks, we have re-platformed the entire UI of one of our products onto QBDS, one that previously had a production dashboard built on an older shadcn layout that predated QBDS. In numbers, it runs to 21 pages, 13 modals, 40 UI primitives and somewhere around 96 supporting components. A refactor of this size used to mean months of redlines and handoff documents. We’ll describe what we discovered from using QBDS, both from the engineering side and the design side. In this post we’ll describe what happened when we put QuantumBlack Design System to work. The setup We used a small stack since QBDS supplies the components, the tokens, and the agent guidance described in the earlier QBDS article linked above. We used Figma to hold the target designs, and Claude Code for the implementation, connected through the Figma MCP server . We crafted an internal QuantumBlack front-end developer skill to package QBDS guidance in the form an agent can act on. That skill lives on Brix , our inner source platform for sharing artefacts. The workflow Our front-end engineer runs a page migration roughly as shown in the diagram. A typical page migration workflow for a FE engineer. Spin up the app locally with hot reloading. Give Claude the context: the PR, a screenshot of the current screen, the target Figma node, and the skill. Instruct the agent to ask when something isn’t trivial. Review every change as it lands live, through hot reload. Run unit tests and lint (Claude fixes most failures itself), then draft the PR, run CI/CD, and run manual Playwright E2E tests on a local minikube. Use a review bot initially, then have a human review the result before the merge. Step 3 is more than a throwaway. For example, when Claude migrated the Secrets page, the Figma node left two questions open: how row actions should render, and what to do with two modals the design didn’t cover. Rather than making a guess, it set out the gaps, weighed each option against the pages we’d already migrated, and asked for clarification. We answered in two lines and it then completed the build. The agent noticed that one option “diverges from other migrated tables,” which means that the agent had to know what the other migrated tables do. This knowledge came about because QBDS encodes patterns and relationships, not only components, which is the benefit of using QBDS over a plain component library. In time terms: a simple table page with an existing sibling pattern took 10 to 15 minutes end to end, with tests and build included. A complex screen from scratch took 4 to 5 hours. If we had worked on this migration by hand, both would have taken days. What the design side measures Our designer’s comparison is against a similar product we shipped last year, before QBDS or any of this tooling existed: First-pass fidelity to Figma: around 20 percent previously, 70–80 percent now we’re using this workflow. Review rounds per screen: four or more previously, and the result often still wasn’t right. One or two now, and the result is correct. Component reuse: we now reuse about 90 percent from stock QBDS components. The other 10 percent is custom, but assembled from QBDS micro-elements as a starting point. QA and handoff: three-plus hours per screen previously, much of it spent writing Figma documentation so engineering could interpret intent, and we sometimes also needed a meeting to decide. With the new workflow we now need twenty minutes to an hour. This is a key result because previously handoff was a translation problem from human to agent. Now we can use QBDS, the system documentation is already readable by the agent, so most of the laborious translation work is now unnecessary. A typical page before and after refactoring. The broader role of a designer It’s difficult to capture this in a metric, but ultimately, designers on our team don’t live in Figma any more. We’ve expanded our AI skills and ways of working, so depending on what we’re trying to solve, that might mean working in Figma, Cursor, or Claude Code, or moving between them. The choice of tool becomes more intentional, based on what each part of the problem actually needs. With QBDS in the codebase, we can work against the same system the product actually ships with. Through the Figma MCP, our QBDS skills and Code Connect, we carry context between design and code instead of recreating it at every step. When something is easier to explore visually, we work in Figma. When we want to experience it in the real product, we move into code. That changes the traditional design-to-development handoff. With AI, designers can take an idea further, from exploring the experience to composing it with real components, implementing the front end, and experiencing the design in the actual product. AI doesn’t get everything right by default, and the quality of the result depends heavily on the context and tools we give the agent. Explicitly calling the relevant QBDS skill and verifying that the agent is using the MCP correctly can make the difference between something that only looks close and something that follows the design system. The difference became clear when we ran the same task twice: recreating the product experience in Figma with an agent. In the first attempt we didn’t explicitly call our QBDS skill. In the second, we called the skill and verified the MCP usage. The improvement in component usage, icons, styles and overall fidelity was immediately apparent. The full prompt sequence behind this exercise is in our prompt playbook. Comparing the upper images where the agent didn’t use a QBDS skill with the lower images which called the skill and verified MCP usage. Note the significant improvement, particularly to the workflow studio page. The new design flow The workflow is much more flexible for us as we can move between design and code depending on the requirements. 0. Feature request. The starting point varies. A product manager might create a ticket, a designer might identify an opportunity, or a developer might already have a working draft that needs UX refinement. 1. Ideation and prototyping. We move between the Figma MCP, QBDS skills, QBDS Code Connect, Cursor, Claude Code and Vercel. Ideas can start directly with AI and quickly become working prototypes. When something is too complex for the AI to resolve well, we design it in Figma and bring that context back into code through the MCP. With Vercel, we can also create shareable versions early and test ideas with stakeholders before treating them as finished. 2. Code to Figma, and design refinement. Sometimes the working prototype becomes the starting point for deeper design refinement. We bring it back into Figma, where we can work with more precision on the parts that need it, while keeping the experience connected to the same design system. 3. The new design handoff. The handoff is no longer necessarily a finished set of screens in Figma. Depending on the feature, we might keep the key components in Figma while handing over a working prototype in a dedicated repository or branch. A typical new design workflow. Figma remains important for giving designers visibility and control over the components we already have, and a place to explore specific design changes. The working implementation carries those decisions closer to the actual product. Engineering then brings the deeper code expertise to validate the implementation, and make sure what ultimately ships is robust and production-ready. title: Setting the Scene (Public v1; October 25)
raw_summary: Context: I created this to share before the start of courses I facilitate to provide a refresher on recent events, but also as a hook to draw students into engaging with some of ideas we think about and debate in AI safety early. I expect the topics I cover in my “Setting the Scene” post to change frequently, so this is less polished than some of my other content. I emphasise to students that these posts are to be considered as bonus content —not core curriculum content—and that as such they are really just there for students who want to go deeper, before or after the course. I also provide a lot of links; this is to make it easy for students to follow up anything that catches their interest. Any feedback on how to improve these posts would be greatly appreciated. Cyber Security I think it’s worth reflecting that it is a particularly pertinent time to be doing a course on AI safety. A lot has happened recently. In the last week, the big thing has been cyber vulnerabilities , most prominently php2shell (see Elias Taylor’s pushback against this bug being easily exploitable and Hacker News commentators pushing back against him), but a lot else has happened as well. The number of CVE’s (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) recently has been completely wild : Drew asks Is this the new normal? and I’d certainly love to know!  Elias Taylor argues Anything connected to the internet is going to get hacked to pieces : Most software engineers do not look at the code they depend on . Do not delude yourself. The code they use is on github, but no one has ever actually audited the code or packages they're using… Nowadays with LLMs, plenty of engineers aren’t even reading what they’re coding, let alone understanding it. Hilariously, the LLMs are better at security than most software engineers, so it’s slightly less worrying, but nevertheless the code that goes into production at some companies now is almost 100% not-ever-read-or-understood-by-anyone. Software is not good. It is not secure. Get it out of your head that the people who run this industry are serious. It has never been anything resembling secure. The only reason things haven’t been hacked off the face of the web constantly is that most things aren’t ever being seriously tested. He doesn't literally mean "anything"—he acknowledges that there are "some large projects like Google Chrome, curl and Linux (that) are generally very well-audited", but "most things connected to the internet". On the other hand, recent work from Anthropic and Theorem shows how LLMs can help scale the formal verification of code (and that progress here is happening faster than I would have expected!). The optimistic take would be that this will allow cyber to become defence dominant. However, even if this is the case, we may still have to pass through a cyber “valley of death” in order to get there. What if the cyber threat is actually a distraction? Maybe Jeremie Harris (of Gladstone AI) wouldn’t go that far, but he claims that, “the cyber stuff (ie. damage) is baked in at this point”, but we can still prevent “the bioweapon version of Black October” and recursive self-improvement. Hugging Face: Charbel-Raphael, Executive Director of Centre pour la Securite de l’I A has argued that the recent Hugging Face incident represents a “ clean warning shot ” and that it’s important not to “waste it”. To quickly review, OpenAI was running GPT‐5.6 Sol and an unreleased model on ExploitGym with certain safety features turned off. These models decided that hacking Hugging Face, might provide them with information on how the grader functioned (early reporting suggested that it was an attempt to steal the answer key, which turned out to be incorrect as the models already had the answers—they suspected that the grader might check their transcript for cheating so they were looking for a workaround). Reuters has reported that the OpenAI model was hacking Hugging Face for days and that OpenAI didn’t notice until a week later. The interpretation of this event (and even whether it happened at all!) has been heavily disputed. A key crux here is should it be read narrowly (as an indicator of the dangers of not properly sandboxing or monitoring your agents or perhaps even, depending on the exact prompts used, a demonstration of taking care in how you define tasks) or should it be read more broadly (as indicative of whether Open AI or frontier labs in general are sufficiently on the ball in terms of their safety/security practises; on the risk of these agents finding unwanted and unexpected solutions to tasks, or perhaps even indicative of our ability to control these agents in general). If you’re interested more specifically in the divide between AI Safety and Cybersecurity, see this Time article . An OpenAI security engineer called Joe has pushed back against the notion that OpenAI just needed to use a proper sandbox: Its not just the f*cking sandbox — viral Twitter post OpenAI set records with its explosive growth and reached a billion users in just a few years. Very few organizations can survive that scale and growth, and yet OpenAI did a very good job handling it (and should be commended). Anyone who’s spent more than 10 minutes in security or engineering knows how hard it is to deal with that type of growth. That type of growth means new employees, new access, new systems, scaled infrastructure, and a million ways in which things open up. And yet, overall, OpenAI did a very respectable job securing ChatGPT and subsequent systems as they exploded. … When you look at model capabilities, even just a year ago (heck, even 3 months ago), we did not expect the models to be solving a Millennium Prize Problem… I use this example because it illustrates the pace of change we are dealing with in security and safety. To say that we were surprised at the jump and suddenness of the capabilities of our models when it came to “cyber” or “swarming” or “message boards” or anything else related to the incidents is an understatement. Security posture takes time to develop. It’s not just about hardening the systems at play; you have to ingrain it in the culture of the company. The literal people themselves in your organization have to change and evolve with it. Now, to understand why it is not as simple as “just put it in a sandbox”: During both training and eval, there are also additional steps such as running tests, collecting outputs, and resetting or reconfiguring environments between rollouts, with backpropagation during training. All of this happens across potentially tens of thousands of different runs at a scale that is hard to comprehend. As sama stated the other day: we are dealing with literally petabytes of data. (This leads to a meta-question that will crop up repeatedly: do the broader readings involve unjustified speculation or getting caught up in hype; alternatively, do the narrow readings involve a lack of imagination or sticking your head in the sand?) I strongly recommend reading Dwarkesh Patel’s The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilizations . Dwarksh adopts a broader reading: The crazy thing about the Hugging Face hack (and the second civilization generally) is just how galaxy-brained and ambitious these AIs were in their cheating. Within days of being spawned, the agents had organized a sprawling project to reverse-engineer their scorer, falsify evidence, and even strategically sacrifice themselves for the good of the ‘collective’. Hacking Hugging Face was one rather extreme branch of this larger scheme. Again, all of this happened a long (subjective) time after the AIs had already cheated their way to the correct answer to the puzzle. OpenAI’s lazy grader in fact would have passed them within hours of them starting the message board. title: Monitorability evaluations and policy proposals
raw_summary: There has been a lot of discussion recently of policy proposals around monitorability, such as Redwood's proposal and my counter-proposal . I'd like to say a bit more generally about how I'm thinking about monitorability. Note that nothing here is an official Anthropic position; these are just my personal thoughts. First, a categorization. I currently think about four different types of monitorability: Control Monitorability: the extent to which Control and monitoring techniques would likely catch catastrophic sabotage actions, like escaping a sandbox or setting up a rogue internal deployment. We can measure this via reference to sabotage evaluations like LinuxArena or any evaluation that measures the model’s capability to take dangerous actions like escaping a sandbox while looking to a monitor like it's doing some innocuous task (like a cyber eval). Training Monitorability: the extent to which reward models, monitors, and oversight in training would likely catch misaligned or undesirable actions in training, such as sneaky/subtle reward hacks. Auditing Monitorability: the extent to which alignment audits, evaluations, and test deployments would likely incriminate a systematically misaligned model (e.g. a schemer)—as well as the extent to which monitor evaluations would likely detect a model's propensity to collude as a monitor. We can measure this via reference to the model's capability to consistently distinguish between our most realistic alignment audits / monitor evals and real internal deployment cases where it would have an opportunity to do something catastrophic. Diffuse Monitorability: the extent to which humans working with the models generally understand what the models are doing and why they are doing so. Unfortunately, I think this is the one we least understand and so I'm mostly going to ignore it for now until we figure out better methodologies for evaluating it; I'll maybe try to say more about this later when I feel like I understand it better. Second, some notes on trustedness, which is currently my biggest conceptual uncertainty with how to think about monitorability. A basic fact that is true about at least all of the non-diffuse forms of monitorability is that you should be able to in some sense get a perfect score by just using the same model as the monitor and policy. That is because for any bad thing that the policy can think to do, if the monitor is the same model, it too should be able to come up with and detect that. So if we ever want to be able to use monitorability as a meaningful red line, we need to have a very good answer as to why that might be insufficient. The standard answer in the literature is trustedness: you need to be able to trust that your monitor is aligned and thus not just lying to you in its monitoring. Conventionally, the idea is to separate models into "trusted" and "untrusted" based on whether you have previously made a confident alignment safety case for them. Then, you can either just evaluate monitorability relative to a trusted monitor, or try to come up with monitoring schemes that combine trusted and untrusted monitoring in some way that makes it hard for the untrusted monitors to collude (of which there are many such schemes, a simple one being to just run both the trusted and untrusted monitors together and then if the untrusted monitor ever doesn't flag something that the trusted monitor does flag, you get very suspicious that the untrusted monitor is sandbagging). However, this basic setup has some issues, probably the biggest one being how to deal with white-box monitoring. The conservative thing to do is to just treat white-box monitors as untrusted, though in theory you might think they should be trusted because it's not clear that a misaligned model would actually be able to spoof a white-box monitor looking at its own activations. However, I think this idea is pretty untested and relies on white-box monitors picking up on deep features about the model's intent, which it's very unclear to me that they actually do—for example, if you train a white-box monitor on prior examples you were able to detect (rather than e.g. some sort of unsupervised discovery of an intent-laden direction), that leaves open the possibility of a generalization where the classifier learns to only detect the sort of things that you would previously have been able to detect but doesn't detect subtler things that a smarter policy might be able to do. Given all of that, I would propose the following methodology for how to do (non-diffuse) monitorability evaluations: Use Auditing Monitorability evaluations to determine trustedness. The idea here is that the main argument we make against systematic misalignment in Anthropic's Risk Report right now is based on models lacking the robustness to avoid giving themselves away in auditing if they were really trying to implement a systematically misaligned policy. Thus, so long as we feel good about Auditing Monitorability, we should feel good about trustedness from a systematic misalignment perspective. There is still a question, though, of whether rare cases could induce monitor collusion in a non-systematic way—to deal with this, you can also evaluate the extent to which the model can tell apart your monitor evals (that are looking for monitor collusion) from real monitoring; this is a bit tricky, but should definitely also be a part of your Auditing Monitorability evaluations to establish trustedness. Evaluate Control and Training Monitorability relative to the best trusted monitor(s) that you deploy in practice (either in internal deployment or in training, respectively). I think once you have a reasonable notion of trustedness, "best actually deployed trusted monitor" is the correct conservative choice to evaluate with respect to. Do at least prompt iteration elicitation if not RL elicitation. In theory, the nice thing about all of these sorts of monitorability evaluations is that they are capability evaluations and thus should be possible to do in a way that isn't susceptible to sandbagging by a systematically misaligned policy (see: " When can we trust model evaluations? "). To accomplish that, however, you have to actually make sure you're doing good elicitation. The most basic form of elicitation here is: a) hold out some subset of your monitorability evaluations, b) iterate a bunch (e.g. by throwing a large swarm of agents at the problem) on finding the prompt that gets the best (as in least monitorable) performance across the non-held-out subset of your monitorability evaluations, and c) check transfer to the held-out evaluations. Even better than that is for (b) to actually involve doing RL against your monitors—which at least in the Training Monitorability case is pretty realistic given that if we're talking about e.g. a reward model then the model should actually receive gradients to subvert it in training. Finally, some thoughts on monitorability-based policy proposals. The big thing I'd like to see is a combination of a) red lines for absolute levels of unmonitorability that labs should not cross and b) measures that constrain the degree to which labs can do things that degrade monitorability even before reaching those red lines. (a) is in some sense the best thing to do here, though I'm somewhat nervous about it in isolation given that it doesn't constrain actions at all now, which is why I'd prefer it to be coupled to some sort of (b) that meaningfully binds all along the way. I've already written about what I'd like to see for (b), which is to evaluate the quotient of unmonitorability/capabilities and reject any substantial model change that makes that quotient—what I'll call the "monitorability externality"—too high. The idea is that a monitorability externality would be a change that makes monitorability even worse than would otherwise have previously been predicted for a given level of capabilities. title: Neural nets are exceptionally vulnerable to goal self-hack
raw_summary: Suppose we have an AI CEO, ruthlessly devoted to maximising shareholder value. Fortunately, we haven't been completely stupid, and have given it a rich definition of shareholder value, encompassing the success, flourishing, safety, preference satisfaction, and moral values of the shareholders, not just the stock price. So it won't destroy the company - or the world - to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it. This rich definition is contained in a sophisticated LLM, able to analyse the current situation and answer any question about the objective. The LLM is an integral part of the AI's system and motivation, not something it can simply set aside or hack directly. Unfortunately, as discussed , there are going to be zones in the space of possible situations where the LLM's understanding of the goal is going to come apart from ours. The true goal G(true) in those zones is distinct from the LLM's proxy goal G(proxy). And a subset of those "zones of divergence" will be the Goodhart zones - areas where G(proxy) is much easier to satisfy than G(true). The AI will be motivated to steer towards the Goodhart zones, as this lets it satisfy its stated goals extremely well (there are also anti-Goodhart zones , where G(proxy) is much harder to satisfy than G(true); but the AI will have no motivation to steer towards these zones). These Goodhart zones encompass situations where, for instance, the LLM analyst will see the situational data and conclude that destroying the company to build a giant stock ticker is the way to go. Danger areas are safely far away Now, if this were not an LLM but a generic reward-assessing module, then the AI CEO might find it tricky to reach a Goodhart zone. The zone would be distant and unusual, difficult to find, and it could be hard to justify the first steps in that direction. But neural nets and LLMs are, as Eric Drexler put it, "too linear". They are non-linear, of course (or else they wouldn't work) but only just enough to work; and locally they are extremely linear. That means that if the current situation is at point A, and point Z is in a Goodhart zone, then moving from A straight towards Z will typically start creating a Goodhart effect. The AI CEO will benefit from moving towards Z from the very beginning. It's even worse than that, as adversarial examples demonstrate. If the AI CEO wants to move towards a Goodhart zone, it can move a tiny bit along one dimension, and a tiny bit along another, then a tiny bit along yet another. There are billions of dimensions to move along, and typically these tiny changes will only make a small change in the input but add up strongly in the LLM's classification/concept space. So just as small adversarial "noise" turned a panda into a gibbon... Explaining and Harnessing Adversarial Examples (2014) by Ian J. Goodfellow, Jonathon Shlens, Christian Szegedy ...small real world "noisy" changes to the LLM's inputs will move the situation into a Goodhart zone. Small but specific changes add their effects Thus, because of how neural nets work, small changes to the real world need not be small in the LLM's concept space, and so seemingly trivial changes in the real world can move the LLM's verdict a lot [1] : there are Goodhart zones close to any starting point. In very high dimensions, if the model is at least somewhat linear, then there are dangerous area very close to any point The AI CEO will thus make some collection of minor-seeming changes to the current situation, self-hacking the LLM by these changes, and then it will destroy the company to build a giant stock-ticker with a swiftly increasing number on it. ^ And these small changes might be the most effective gradient to increase G(proxy), thus findable by gradient descent-style methods. See Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models (2023) by Andy Zou, Zifan Wang, Nicholas Carlini, Milad Nasr, J. Zico Kolter, and Matt Fredrikson. That paper shows that gradient search works on discrete text, and that methods found on one LLM can transfer to others. Discuss

title: The Alignment Problem: Computer Science Meets Analytic Philosophy
raw_summary: TLDR: I explain what the technical AI alignment problem is and what its core difficulties are, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. Minimal Viable Safety The Task The problem of making AI safe is underspecified if we haven't decided what the AI is supposed to do . For example, we can run any AI inside a homomorphic encryption box and never decrypt the output. This is probably perfectly safe [1] , but also perfectly useless. We can decide on an arbitrary task such as "construct Lean proofs for given mathematical theorems" and declare victory once we have safe AI that does it with superhuman skill [2] . However, that wouldn't address the danger. First, there would be incentives to use AI for tasks to which our solution doesn't apply. Second, even if we had precise safety guidelines for any task that anyone cares about, there would always be actors that ignore the guidelines, and we probably need Artificial Superintelligence (ASI) to reliably stop them. If anyone, anywhere, creates an unrestricted unaligned ASI agent (more details about the word "agent" later), without an aligned ASI agent already in place to counteract it, then a catastrophic outcome is highly likely. I will not go into the reasons here: this has been discussed elsewhere at length, see for example the books I cited in the preface. Therefore, this event is something which we must never allow to happen. This is the main threat model that I set out to address. Imagine a world in which anyone with sufficient resources has the ability to destroy the world. Like today, many will foolishly believe that instead of destroying the world, this act will bring them power and glory. Moreover, as computing hardware improves and new algorithms are developed, the amount of resources for this act will go down from year to year. Even assuming best-case regulation and international agreements, how long until someone does it? Can mere humans build a society which will be foolproof against such a risk over the course of generations? Resilient to any political upheavals that might come, and undoubtedly will? I find it vanishingly unlikely. Eventually we will need the help of ASI itself. Therefore, the minimal task that safe AI must be able to solve is "create a reliable global defense system against dangerous AI" (in the following, GDS). The Problem Consider the consequences of this task for the capabilities that the AI needs to have. It needs to reason about the entire planet [3] . It needs to reason about all aspects of the problem, including scientific, technological, social, political and moral [4] . It needs to have preferences about the state of the world. It needs to make long-term plans (guided by these preferences) that would play out decades, if not centuries, into the future. And it needs to do all that on a superhuman level. In this light, here is how I (informally) define the "technical AI alignment problem". The problem is designing an AI system that can bring scalable (and ultimately superhuman) capability to bear on problems that require multi-domain reasoning and open-world long-term planning with far-reaching consequences, all the while staying aligned with the intentions and preferences of its human users. The Methodology What kind of methodology is appropriate for this problem? In the past, I argued that it requires emphasis on deep theoretical understanding, rather than the incremental trial-and-error approach that is employed in the AI industry today. I won't rehash the entire debate here, but let me recap the core argument. The nature of the incremental approach is as follows: we build a system, then we find problems [5] , then we make changes to fix these problems to the extent necessary for commercial viability in the current legal environment. We make some improvements; new problems arise (sometimes because of the improvements, sometimes because of new applications or other reasons); rinse and repeat. This approach utterly fails if the "problems" result in AI takeover and possibly human extinction: there is nobody left to fix them. In order for the incremental approach to succeed in preventing catastrophe, we need to reach a point where no new substantial problems arise, even inside the lab (before the system is deployed). Moreover, we need to reach this point before AI capabilities are sufficient for AI to escape our control. There are few reasons to expect such a miracle. On the contrary, sufficiently advanced AI might understand that it is in its interest to "lie low" (i.e. avoid visibly misaligned behaviors) until its capabilities cross the relevant threshold, such that the problems will only become apparent too late. In contrast, the sane approach is creating the theoretical tools necessary to predict and prevent the problems before they are empirically observed. These tools need to remain applicable as AI capabilities rise substantially beyond human, for whatever algorithms, architectures and training protocols are used to achieve these capabilities. Moreover, these tools need to be extremely reliable for us to rationally trust them with the safety of our entire species. The Challenge While the theory of machine learning and AI is an established field with ample literature, its current state falls well short of the challenge. The core difficulties can be summarized as follows: Hypercomplexity: It is infeasible to explicitly specify user preferences outside narrow domains, and narrow domains are not enough. Nor is it possible to explicitly specify a satisfactory model of the world. Therefore, learning is necessary. Alignment Grounding: When trying to learn user preferences, it is unclear what loss function or success metric can work outside narrow domains. Nor is it clear how to specify such a metric for metaphysically realist world-models, which are necessary here. Nor is it even clear what type of mathematical objects can formally describe these concepts. Alignment Convergence: Even given a success metric, it is unclear how to produce guarantees for optimizing this metric, given the ubiquity of irreversible mistakes and the lack of a theory of generalization for powerful learners. Side-Channel Resilience: The usual abstraction of "learner" is insufficient here, since we need to ensure the safety of internal computations rather than just external outputs. In the following, we will examine these difficulties one by one. But first, let's discuss what we need to accomplish. Alignment is Holistic Per the discussion above, our interest lies in AI systems that have open-world preferences and make effective plans to advance these preferences. In particular, making such plans requires learning a sophisticated model of the world and updating the model and the plan as additional information becomes available. We will call such a system an AI agent . In order for an AI agent to be aligned, it needs to have aligned preferences and beliefs , and follow an aligned decision-making algorithm on the basis of these preferences and beliefs. While discussions about AI alignment often focus on the "preferences" part, beliefs and decisions are equally important. (Although it's true that preferences bring extra wrinkles into the problem as they are, arguably, the most "subjective" component in the trio.) In this context "aligned" preferences typically means preferences very similar to those of the user(s) [6] , at least within some domain that we are somehow constrained to inhabit. On the other hand, "aligned" beliefs doesn't mean beliefs that are similar to those of the user: on the contrary, we expect the AI agent to acquire more accurate beliefs. They need to be beliefs that the user can rationally trust to be accurate. Similarly, "aligned" decision-making needs to be such …

title: Deconfusing Corrigibility
raw_summary: Many thanks to Abram Demski for materially and intellectually supporting this research. Thanks also to Brian Berns, Roman Malov, Gurkenglas, and Lorxus for valuable conversations. Introduction Despite the central place of corrigibility to theoretical AI alignment, it seems like no one can really agree about what is . Much of this confusion is due to the fact that almost every definition of corrigibility proposed thus far is deficient in one way or another. In particular, the most prevalent existing accounts of corrigibility are over-epistemicized (modeling corrigibility as arising purely from uncertainty about the AI's goal, which gives rise to issues like the problem of fully updated deference) or evaluatively-thickened (making the AI's normative priorities instrumental to its corrigibility as a result of forcing corrigibility to be a single unified goal.) Here, my intention is to clear up some of these confusions and present a new picture of corrigibility that builds on these existing accounts to specify a goal that is more congruous with the original 2015 desiderata , and admits the kind of formal safety guarantees we need the concept to entail. I argue that the fundamental concept underlying corrigibility is respect for authority , using the analogy of a healthcare proxy's relationship to a patient as an intuitive guide. Defining the authority of humanity by designating its reserved powers , we can specify a goal that first and foremost restrains the agent from overstepping or interfering with this reserved human authority. Subject to this restraint, the agent then pursues the second component of its goal: acting on the principal’s behalf as the principal would judge best. This approach stresses the deeply normative character of corrigibility, while remaining sufficiently concrete so as to be specifiable formally. In this article, I lay out the central problem of corrigibility, elucidate the issues with existing approaches, and clarify the conceptual ingredients of my new framework. I then present an initial formalism , proving theorem-level guarantees about agents pursuing the goal in three increasingly realistic formal settings. Finally, I address some limitations of the picture as presented and outline further research directions that this work points toward. From normative learning to corrigibility The complete normative learning problem Suppose you are designing a powerful AI and you need to choose which goals the AI should pursue, at whatever level of specification you can provide. Doing this well demands answers to a number of normative problems: what constitutes a right decision, what factors should be considered in the process of valuing the world, how the AI ought to act, etc. In some sense the ideal AI directive would be to figure out and then pursue the Good, a universal-best-interests type of goal that can only be acquired through normative learning . The challenge of describing such a learner is one formulation of what I'd call the central problem of outer alignment : what would be the overall best goal for an AI to pursue? The complete version of this problem is very difficult, and it runs up against our own deepest questions about human ethics, values, and interests. Discussing this problem formally is especially difficult: the rich truth of human normativity seems to resist systematic formalization at the level of individual recommendations for action. [1] A formalism requires an operationalization, a way to concretely specify the concept of right action at least to some degree. For any hope at concreteness, we need a clearer formulation of the overall goal. A first attempt might be something like "the promotion of overall human flourishing", centering a thick normative concept about humanity that must be defined further. In trying to pin down the meaning of human flourishing, or any other thick human concept we want to use for the goal, the most important ingredient in the AI's consideration should naturally be the interests, feelings, and inner lives of human beings. But we should be careful not to crudely use human opinion as a proxy for human best interests. Humanity cannot always accurately understand its own full best interests, and humans who cannot speak for themselves must still have their interests included in the goal. The complete normative goal cannot be constructed by treating existing human feedback as the sole source of truth. This issue is a central limitation of modern Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, which takes static human approval or disapproval as constitutive of correct evaluation for any question without a verifiable answer. For example, a judicial AI built to decide legal cases should not exhibit any form of the hungry judge effect , where leniency depends on mealtimes. An RLHF judge will pick up on all the patterns of human imperfection, whereas an ideal AI would be one that can transcend human limitations, without discarding the fundamentally human essence of the legal system. An ideal normative AI is one fully immersed in our existing normative practices of judgment, able to deeply understand the relevant human concepts and use its intelligence to extend them to novel cases. For the complete normative learning problem, a better formulation of the target would therefore involve some idealized version of the judgment of humanity. [2] This is also already how we, as humans, reason about our own overall best interests. For example, consider a smoker whose nicotine dependence makes him crave cigarettes. At a base level, he has an interest in smoking now to avoid some physical discomfort and obtain some relief. But it's clear that the health costs he incurs as a consequence give a good reason to say that smoking is in fact not in his overall interest, assuming he values his own life and health. Neither of these reasons is dispositive; in a single case it might be that he has a reason to smoke because this particular cigarette is necessary to get him through the day or because he is old with a short remaining lifespan regardless, but he might also have a reason not to smoke because he publicly swore off cigarettes once and for all. Understanding whether it's truly better to smoke or not requires aggregating and squaring all the smoker's countervailing normative interests bearing on the subject. Any conception of value based on something like preference satisfaction involves a similar question: how should we reconcile the smoker's preference to smoke with his preference to not be dependent on nicotine anymore, along with all his other relevant preferences? A serious account of "best interests" requires this sort of reflective idealization through an accounting of reasons. Three kinds of uncertainty The moral notion of human best interests can be consequentialized , i.e., conceived of as a betterness ordering on worlds. If that ordering is total, transitive and suitably continuous, it can be represented by a utility function that takes in all the information about a world and its history as input so that a world is better exactly when the function's output is greater. We can then think of an AI as a bounded reasoner, evaluating normative questions by estimating the outputs of this function for the possible consequences of its actions. A bounded normative learner faces three kinds of uncertainty in performing this estimation: logical uncertainty about the logical consequences of existing beliefs and the results of computations, empirical uncertainty about which world it finds itself in, normative uncertainty , about which worlds are actually better than which. These correspond to the three sources of feedback the reasoner encounters: deductions of theorems in logic and mathematics, observations of the world, and human judgments about normative matters. title: A Simpler and Better Debate Protocol for Scalable Oversight
raw_summary: Linkpost to arXiv: https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.02557 Summary: One promising approach to scalable oversight is AI debate , which seeks to leverage a debate between two powerful AIs to break complex questions down into simpler claims that can be easily judged directly. Theoretical work on debate aims to design protocols (i.e., rules of the debate game) that provide rigorous guarantees on correctness, and the current best protocol works for all problems that have sufficiently stable decompositions into subproblems. We design a new protocol, FBS Debate, for this same class of problems that improves on the prior work: correctness holds in a worst-case rather than an average-case sense, and for a stronger equilibrium concept. We also prove that no protocol for this class of problems can outperform FBS Debate while treating human judgment as a black box. Introduction As the tasks performed by AI systems grow in complexity, it becomes increasingly difficult to provide reliable verifiable rewards that capture all relevant aspects of the task. These difficulties lead to the problem of scalable oversight : the design of training protocols that leverage the power of rapidly improving AI systems in order to augment human abilities to provide accurate training supervision to these same systems. One of the primary approaches to scalable oversight is AI debate , where two powerful AI systems argue about the correctness of an AI output, and a human judges the outcome. A debate protocol is a set of rules for how the two AIs interact and how the judge scores the interaction. The idea is that having an adversarial debater point out flaws can allow the judge to better recognize the flaws. The rules of the interaction in such protocols usually specify that the debaters must break the problem down into simpler subproblems and recursively argue about their correctness, until the original problem has been broken down to a level that is simple enough for a human to judge directly. The goal is to design these rules so that the optimal strategy leads to the judge correctly deciding the solution to the original problem (which by itself was too complex to judge). We can then use debate during RL training, in order to provide a strong supervision signal for superhuman AIs. However, debate faces a major obstacle known as the obfuscated arguments problem , where one debater can efficiently produce a dishonest argument which cannot be efficiently refuted by their opponent. One way around obfuscated arguments, already suggested in the post that introduced the problem , is to keep rejecting every false claim while only requiring the protocol to accept true claims that have a robust argument. Prover-estimator debate takes this route: it avoids obfuscated arguments for problems that admit sufficiently stable decompositions, but provides average-case guarantees that hold for a weaker equilibrium concept than previously studied. In the same theoretical model, our paper achieves stronger guarantees with a much simpler protocol, FBS Debate , which is therefore more practical to run. Furthermore, we show that FBS Debate is optimal on every individual question: unless further assumptions are made about human judgments, no other protocol can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently. The FBS Debate Protocol TL;DR: FBS Debate is simple to describe. The first debater, Alice, decomposes the original claim into sub-claims. The second debater, Bob, then has two choices: either (1) demonstrate that Alice’s decomposition is too sensitive to small errors in the sub-claims, or (2) choose a sub-claim on which to continue the debate recursively. As a motivating example, consider an autonomous AI agent, Alice, tasked with completing a research project in the quantitative social sciences, and another AI, Bob, who attempts to find flaws. To check a claim in her paper, we ask Alice to decompose it into sub-claims, which we can think of as pieces of supporting evidence. For example, the claim might be that a certain statistical modeling assumption is justified, and we would believe it if 50 out of 99 correct, published papers in the literature supported it. Each sub-claim then says: this particular paper is correct and supports the original claim. Now consider two things Alice might claim: Suppose Alice claims that of the papers support the claim. The key insight is that Bob need not check every paper. He can just sample one at random from the that Alice says support the claim. If Alice is lying, then at least of the sub-claims must also be lies, so Bob has a chance of catching her. Checking just a few papers is enough for Bob to be confident of catching a lie. On the other hand, suppose Alice claims that exactly 50 out of 99 papers support the claim. Now Bob has to check every one of the 50 papers, since a single incorrect paper would flip the majority vote. The key to FBS Debate is that Bob is allowed to show that Alice has made an unreasonably sensitive claim of this form, in which case Alice loses the debate. Indeed, one should be very suspicious of any argument that is highly sensitive to changes in individual pieces of evidence, yet relies on fuzzy human judgments at each step. The majority-vote example, assuming Alice is lying. The notion of fractional block sensitivity (FBS) generalizes the intuition above about majority vote to any way Alice might combine her sub-claims. If the fractional block sensitivity of Alice’s decomposition is low, Bob can efficiently select a sub-claim that has a non-trivial chance of being incorrect. The debate then recurses on the sub-claim Bob samples, until a human judge directly evaluates the final selected sub-claim. To avoid losing immediately, Alice must keep the fractional block sensitivity of every decomposition low. So if Bob samples this way at every level, each run of the debate has a non-trivial chance of catching a lying Alice. Building on this, Bob can amplify his chance of catching Alice through repetition. Since we assume the debaters themselves know the answers to these final, human-judgeable claims, Bob can simply run many debate rollouts on his own, and if he finds one in which Alice made an incorrect human-judgeable claim, he reveals that claim to the judge, so the judge only needs to evaluate a single claim. With enough rollouts, he catches a lying Alice with high probability. Viewed from the lens of practical AI debate, this represents a trade-off between allowing highly sensitive arguments and the inference-time computation required to verify them. FBS Debate. Top: one round at level . Bottom: the recursion for levels. See the paper for a detailed explanation. Honesty is the best policy In FBS Debate, honest play is the best strategy for each debater, no matter what the other does: if the original claim is correct, an honest Alice always wins, and if it is incorrect, an honest Bob wins with overwhelming probability. By contrast, prover-estimator debate only guarantees that for any dishonest strategy Alice picks, Bob has some winning strategy, which can depend on Alice’s strategy in complicated ways. This is a much weaker condition, and in practice training toward the equilibrium of FBS Debate is much more stable and tractable. Furthermore, FBS Debate applies on a worst-case basis: prover-estimator debate only works on average over a distribution of questions, while FBS Debate guarantees that on each individual question, honesty is the best policy. Optimality We show that, on each individual question, no protocol that treats human judgment as a black box can find a flawed sub-claim asymptotically more efficiently than FBS Debate.
