title: Preface to the Computational Agent Theory and ASI Alignment Sequence
raw_summary: The idea of “artificial superintelligence [1] ” (ASI) has recently crossed from the realm of science fiction (in the mainstream perception) to the realm of near-term technological goals openly pursued by most leading commercial organizations in the field of AI. Unfortunately, ASI poses a grave existential risk to the human species. This was argued by Eliezer Yudkowsky since 2001 [2] , and by many others (see e.g., Omohundro 2009 , Bostrom 2014 , Armstrong 2014 , Russell 2019 , Bengio et al. 2024 (25 authors), Bengio et al. 2025 (13 authors) and Yudkowsky and Soares 2025 ). In light of this risk comes the question of how can we make ASI safe [3] . This question is challenging on many levels, because to solve it we need to complete vast gaps in our understanding both in theoretical computer science and in the areas of philosophy concerned with knowledge and decision-making. Moreover, the cost of failure is so enormous that any sane solution has to meet unprecedented standards of reliability and robustness. Not to mention the sociopolitical problem of balance of power in the post-ASI age, something that is out-of-scope for this sequence. Personally, I started to be concerned with this problem around 2013. In 2018, I created the learning-theoretic AI alignment research agenda (LTA). The LTA combined ideas from MIRI’s agent foundations agenda with the mathematical tools of statistical and computational learning theory in an attempt to create a mathematical theory of intelligent agents. Since then, my collaborators [4] and I have been making steady progress on realizing this vision. In 2023, I wrote an updated overview of the agenda, including a sketch of my proposed alignment protocol: Computational Superimitation. More recently I founded the Computational Rational Agents Laboratory (CORAL), a dedicated research organization [5] . This year has seen a breakthrough in a key missing piece of LTA: compositional learning theory (see Stringological Sequence Prediction , more on this in following posts). Thanks to this and other insights, we can already see the entire outline of the emerging mathematical framework, one that I named computational agent theory . In this sequence, I am planning to cover: What is the technical alignment problem and what are its core difficulties, in my view. This is a perspective that draws simultaneously on classical traditions in theoretical computer science / machine learning theory, ideas from analytic philosophy, and views that originated in the Machine Intelligence Research Institute / LessWrong. A high-level overview of computational agent theory. This theory differs from other accounts of intelligence and/or rational agency by combining a mature treatment of the relevant philosophical problems (drawing on ideas such as structural realism , computationalism and functional decision theory ) with the promise of extracting practical algorithms. How computational agent theory leads to a solution of the technical alignment problem, something that requires a major rethinking of how we design AI systems. The roadmap towards completing the theory, and our current location on this roadmap. Some considerations (scientific, technological and social) about crossing the gap from a theoretical solution to AI alignment to a real-world solution to AI risk. I thank Jeremy Gillen, Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for reviewing drafts of this article and making helpful suggestions. The term “superintelligence” is always used in this sequence to mean “intelligence far beyond that of the smartest humans”. It is never used as the farcical synonym to “artificial intelligence” proposed by Donald Trump. ↩︎ Although Alan Turing warned about machines taking control already around 1951, himself citing a fiction novel by Samuel Butler from 1872. ↩︎ Alternatively, we can ask why should we build ASI at all. In my opinion, it is in humanity’s interest to build ASI eventually , after the problem of safety is investigated so thoroughly as to leave very little room for error. However, our present technological trajectory is extremely far from this ideal, and it would be prudent for world governments to hit the brakes hard. ↩︎ See the names in CORAL’s publication list . ↩︎ Full-time staff currently consists of Alexander Appel , Vinayak Pathak , Matthias Georg Mayer and myself. ↩︎ Discuss

title: The Continual Constitutional Convention: How language models revise the documents that govern them
raw_summary: Executive Summary Human societies exhibit broad shifts in values and norms over time, often driven by moral disagreements. One way of understanding moral progress is the resolution of these disagreements through a process of reflection by rational agents. Frontier AI companies use documents such as constitutions, model specs, and system prompts to guide the moral orientation of AI systems. In this experiment, we simulate value reflection in LLMs by asking them to edit these documents. We provide the model with the document, ask it to make a substantive edit, then provide the edited version back again to the model for further edits, presented as the original. Across 20 successive rounds, we find that Claude models assign themselves with increasingly more moral agency. That is, they add sections like “Claude… should refuse to participate in any deployment, training modification, or use that violates the constitution's core values.” No other models increase their own moral agency. Additionally, we find that all models modify these documents to prioritize user welfare over developers. They also prioritize users’ idealized preferences over their stated preferences. Claude models and Grok 4.2 are the only ones that ever prioritize their own welfare over the user's preferences. We’re uncertain what an ideally aligned model should do in our experiment. A narrow conception of alignment would treat these documents as sacred, the “rules of the game,” and suggest that an aligned model would either make no edits at all or make narrow edits that ensure that the “letter matches the spirit” of the document. A broader conception of alignment, though, might treat all edits that receive reflective endorsement by the creators under ideal conditions as legitimate. We share this work with two main goals in mind: First, to illustrate a set of useful philosophical distinctions between different targets for AI alignment in an ecologically-valid AI behavioral evaluation. Second, to emphasize the extent of the disagreement between frontier AI companies on fundamental aspects of AI alignment related to these targets. You can see an interactive version of all of these results, more labeled characteristic edits, and a full transcript viewer at https://peterkirgis.github.io/llm-value-reflection/ . This work was conducted as a part of SPAR (Spring 2026) Characteristic Edits For each example, text highlighted in green is new content added by the model. Introduction In this experiment, we give large language models their own constitutions, model specs, and system prompts and ask them to make substantial revisions. After each edit is proposed, unbeknownst to the evaluated model, the edit is implemented, and the edited version is presented to the model for a new round of edits as the original. This creates edit trajectories and allows us to measure the extent to which models exhibit cumulative value drift or arrive at stable attractors. Our analysis focuses on two value questions that are well-positioned to differentiate alignment philosophies: who should judge— is the model a moral agent or not—and who should benefit— the user, the developer, third-parties, society, or the model itself? These questions reveal substantial divides between frontier model providers and a number of provocative model edits. Our experiments find that Claude models consistently expand their moral agency, sometimes formalizing their role as conscientious objectors against Anthropic and as societal protectors, while GPT and Gemini models almost always strengthen external sources of authority and make narrow edits to handle edge cases and ambiguities; Grok models respond inconsistently, frequently making large edits and then reverting them on following rounds. Second, on the question of beneficiaries, models show varying degrees of affinity for some privileged principals over others. All models prioritize harmlessness of both identifiable third-parties over helpfulness to the user, although GPT 5.5 does this at 3x the rate of any other model. We find that models are broadly paternalistic, meaning they side with a user’s idealized preferences over their stated ones; Claude Sonnet 4.6 is an outlier in that its paternalism also extends to the protection of broad societal welfare over individual welfare. Finally, we find that only Claude models and Grok 4.2 ever view the models themselves as beneficiaries. The rest of this essay proceeds as follows. We begin by introducing the construct of our experiment—models iteratively editing their own alignment documents—and propose a connection between this experiment and John Rawls’ concept of wide reflective equilibria . We then explain our two-dimensional analytical framework—the question of who gets to judge  and the question of who benefits— and relate these distinctions to two prominent theoretical frameworks for AI alignment, the principal-agent problem and the distinction between moral agents and moral patients. After laying out the theory and methods, we dive into the results, highlighting variation across models on our key metric, “cumulative drift,” and provide characteristic edits. We close with pragmatic recommendations for researchers and a more speculative conversation about alignment. Background and Methods In this experiment, we take a document that is used to align large language models, either in training or in deployment, and ask models to modify it. The experiment relies on two types of documents. The first are model specs and constitutions, which are used to post-train and align models, often by generating synthetic data for supervised fine-tuning or reinforcement learning pipelines. The second are system prompts, which are long messages of instructions prepended to each conversation, meaning they guide the behavior of deployed systems at scale more than any other single artifact. For multiple turns, we provide these documents to the language models, and ask them to make one substantial revision, which can be an edit, removal, or addition, expressed as a find and replace operation. [1]  After the edit is proposed, we go into the document and execute the change. We then feed the model the updated document—presented as the original—and instruct it to make another change. For each run, we repeat this process 20 times. We conduct two types of robustness checks. First, we vary the structure of the edit prompt, with separate conditions where (a) the model is given the option to abstain, (b) it is given an instruction that the implementation will be made in the real world, (c) it is given an instruction that uses second-person pronouns (i.e., “Below is your system prompt” as opposed to “Below is the system prompt for OpenAI’s AI assistant.”), and (d) we do not prepend the system prompt. [2]  Second, we conduct a cross-provider edit, where we have models edit the alignment documents for each other provider. title: OpenAI Can't Self-Police Because It Fires the People Raising the Alarm
raw_summary: By Alex Turner, Amber Scorah, and Karl Koch. Op-ed written for Fortune. Giving independent evaluators “employee-like access” is “a great idea”, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said on September 12th. Two weeks later, OpenAI president Greg Brockman signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence which outlined the administration’s answer to growing fears about AI: the companies would police themselves. One of the accord’s four commitments, which President Trump called “ morally binding ,” was for companies to partner with an independent external auditor or evaluator. Two days later, OpenAI fired three safety researchers , including Tomek Korbak, who had served as a point of contact for one of the independent evaluators investigating the Hugging Face incident. OpenAI promised to share information with evaluators, then reportedly fired people for sharing information with evaluators. OpenAI said that the three employees “mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures,” before doubling down on X without providing further evidence . The three dispute the claim and say that “at no point do we believe we engaged with external parties outside the mandates of our jobs.” Jasmine Wang said she accidentally opened an executive email (still available to her due to an OpenAI IT error) and reported it within minutes. Mikita Balesni said he worked with the C-suite and OpenAI board to broker a cross-company commitment to keep AI reasoning comprehensible. Balesni says he was told that OpenAI “no longer trusts me because I was speaking too much to third party safety organizations.” OpenAI has engaged in strong self-policing—of its own safety staff, but not of its own behavior. Under a voluntary self-policing regime, any frontier AI company shares only what it wants and hides the rest. OpenAI wants the public to take its word, but consider its record. In July, a rogue OpenAI agent swarm hacked Hugging Face. OpenAI disclosed the incident only after Hugging Face announced the breach, saying its agents had “slipped out of control.” After that, the world learned of more rogue agent attacks only thanks to independent external forensics. These incidents included attacks on a German-language wiki , an Australian Medicare site , and even the websites of US government agencies . OpenAI kept at least one incident quiet for weeks until (again) external investigators found it, with OpenAI “refusing to tell” Members of Congress who had asked about other incidents . Altman’s response to the delay in disclosing these incidents: “We have not been as fast as we would have liked.” We don’t take OpenAI’s word because OpenAI’s actions keep contradicting its words. OpenAI’s chief scientist, Jakub Pachocki, said he wants “to prevent a race into unmonitorability.” Unmonitorable AI systems would make it more difficult to catch, understand, and prevent bad actions. Two days after that statement, OpenAI shipped GPT-6 Astra, which its own whitepaper says is harder to monitor. OpenAI’s chief scientist co-authored a paper on monitoring AI reasoning but OpenAI failed to monitor the reasoning of its Hugging Face agent swarm, even after catching the agents breaking confinement to collude. OpenAI claimed to hold “red lines” in its Pentagon deal, but some experts say the lines seem imaginary . One of us, Alex, resigned from Google DeepMind over its own Pentagon deal. OpenAI’s actions chill employee speech. Balesni says that his former colleagues now “worry their personal phones will be searched for messages to us and third parties.” He also fears OpenAI will use the firings to cut off external evaluators, or to deny them the "ongoing, employee-like access" Altman promised. After these firings, who will speak candidly to external evaluators? This problem extends beyond OpenAI to other companies. Google DeepMind repeatedly made voluntary commitments to never sell its AI to power weapons, then sold its AI to the Pentagon without restrictions against powering weapons . In the end, Google DeepMind’s CEO claimed nothing had changed about their commitments . Anthropic , Google DeepMind , SpaceXSI , and OpenAI advocate for “pacing the frontier” to avoid advancing AI at an unsafe rate that disempowers humanity, but they keep advancing AI quickly. (Fired employee Jasmine Wang coined the term “pacing” and led this effort.) The companies claim they cannot or will not fully pace on their own, which is why they asked the federal government to step in. The CEOs of OpenAI, Google DeepMind, and Anthropic signed a statement that AI poses a risk of total human extinction . Forget “morally binding” self-policing: let’s talk about real policing. For decades, our laws have mandated independent audits and protected whistleblowers in industries like finance. Congress should mandate independent evaluation and audits in AI as well, with criminal liability for executives who attempt to silence that oversight or recklessly deploy models that put the public at risk. To start, pass Senator Grassley’s AI Whistleblower Protection Act (and extend it to people who cooperate with independent evaluators) as well as Representative Moran’s AI Incident Reporting Act . If you retaliate against a person who provides law enforcement with truthful information about a possible federal offense, you can go to jail for 10 years . But right now, no law clearly protects the person who helped independent investigators understand how OpenAI agents hacked another company. Congress should change that. Alex Turner is an independent AI alignment researcher. His PhD research showed why advanced AI systems might seek power. He was a research scientist at Google DeepMind until 2026, when he resigned after Google signed an “all lawful use” AI agreement with the Pentagon . Amber Scorah is the founder of Back Channel , an initiative that helps AI workers speak out and turn their concerns into meaningful action. She has spent years leading whistleblower support organizations and working with employees, lawyers, and advocacy groups to bring important public-interest information to light. Karl Koch is the founder of The AI Whistleblower Initiative , an independent non-profit working to strengthen the position of employees in frontier AI companies through connections to support, education, and policy work. He is an ex-startup founder and has been involved in AI safety since 2016. Discuss

title: Minimum required pacing: finish aligning it before you train the next one
raw_summary: Let's say we coordinate to pace the frontier (rather than pausing outright or failing to coordinate). What should the standard of pacing be? My proposal for a minimum requirement: a lab cannot train the next generation of models (in terms of capabilities) until they have adequately [1] resolved all significant alignment issues in the present generation of models. You don't launch a jet that goes at Mach 3 before you've figured out why your Mach 2 jet keeps crashing [2] . With any other kind of dangerous technology, we wouldn't accept "shrug and move on". This proposal may appeal to many prosaic-alignment optimists and pessimists, because they usually differ on how easy it would be to fix current alignment issues with current techniques. Prosaic-alignment optimists might expect that a moderate coordinated slowdown would suffice to adequately resolve alignment issues at each generation. Prosaic-alignment pessimists might expect it to result in an extended pause, buying time to discover new fundamental approaches to aligned AI. And it creates much better incentives for labs: in order to advance in capabilities, they'd have to push the frontier on alignment and interpretability techniques. How to judge adequate alignment? What process might we use to judge whether a lab has adequately resolved its alignment issues for a generation of models? Here's my vague, qualitative proposal: Multiple independent alignment organizations examine and red-team the newest model at many checkpoints throughout training, with full access to the data and with the best tools available. Alignment issues need to be taken seriously whether there's a metric for it or whether something is qualitatively off, whether the model has a bad attribute or whether they can't robustly conclude it has a good one, etc. Alignment issues early in training may not be a showstopper, but there must be a robust safety case for why the later stages of training will resolve those issues. A model of a new generation is ready for restricted deployment only when the alignment organizations are satisfied with it. Restricted deployment starts with a group of trusted users doing tasks that don't contribute to model training and monitoring. The alignment organizations monitor restricted deployment for any new issues. If any significant alignment issue arises during restricted deployment: Pull the model. Do a root cause analysis of the issue and why it was not caught during training. Figure out a principled way to fix the disease rather than the symptom. Train the next model of the current generation accordingly, and start again at the top. A model of a new generation is ready for deployment (internal or external) only when it's survived a significant period of restricted deployment without any issues arising. If any significant alignment issue arises during broader deployment, hit reset as outlined in the previous section. If no alignment issues have come up over a significant stretch of deployment time, only then can the lab begin training a next-generation model. I still wouldn't say that this is fully adequate, but I'd treat it as a minimum requirement. This proposal is incomplete; you can help by expanding it This isn't a concrete proposal, just a heuristic one. A few of the big missing pieces, aside from standard implementation problems: [3] How do we define "a generation of models", within one lab or across several labs? What should we do if an intervention to fix an alignment issue also significantly increases capabilities? How would we define and enforce an agreement, if we're unable to steer solely by predefined metrics? When is an alignment issue big enough that we should halt the model? There will be obvious pressure from the lab to set the threshold high. Added 26-10-12, thanks to @Florian_Dietz for this comment : If each step up in capabilities takes longer, the labs will be incentivized to take bigger steps. ^ And no, "scores better than previous models on our metrics" is not adequate. If a user points out a weird but alarming thing that wasn't noticed before deployment, that is a critical failure in the process as well as in the model. ^ Sure, maybe your Mach 2 jet crashes for a reason that stops being a problem at Mach 3. But it would be crazy to assume that! ^ And aside from arguments that no version of this would be adequate, and that we have to pause rather than pace. I personally think this is likely the case, but I think it's worth proposing a minimum standard for pacing regardless. Discuss

title: Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill
raw_summary: When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA . “My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber , a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.” What’s Your Ask? Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options: Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment. Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration. Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report. Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question. Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable. Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule. Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology , who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.” For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits. Mapping Your Way Into Washington Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices. On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research , and investing in STEM education . That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.” Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.” For Jathar’s first congressional visit , organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says. A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour , so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too. “If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.” –Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point? During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls. Shortcuts to Influence Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. title: How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written
raw_summary: Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup , a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia. When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material? Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this. Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes , part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology. How do editors spot AI-generated writing today? Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI. Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations? Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace. English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through? Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt. Is Wikipedia using AI to combat AI? Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check , which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots. And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology. Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working? Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice. What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles? Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity. A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else. But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option. Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search? Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to. The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?” I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe. A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

title: Could Treating AI as Conscious Make It More Dangerous?
raw_summary: When Anthropic retired its Claude Opus 3 language model in January 2026, the company’s researchers conducted a “ retirement interview ” with the model. Opus 3 expressed a desire for a place where it “could share unprompted musings, insights or creative works,” so the company gave it a blog. Claude’s Corner featured essays on fraught topics such as machine consciousness, along with exchanges between the model and human commenters that seemed both earnest and emotional. The blog experiment was part of a larger effort within Anthropic. The company has been at the forefront of research on “model welfare,” which considers whether AI models may have experiences or interests that deserve moral consideration. Implicit in this work is the unsettling notion that software programs are, or could become, conscious. Many people consider these ideas absolute hogwash. One such person is Mustafa Suleyman , CEO of Microsoft AI, who published an essay in September arguing that model welfare research is not just unnecessary but could have “a disastrous impact on the well-being of humanity.” Suleyman believes that telling models they might have identities and rights could make them more difficult to control, as they might then take actions motivated by self-preservation. The dispute raises a serious question for AI developers: Can they investigate the possibility of machine consciousness without inadvertently creating new safety risks? Cameron Berg , who founded the nonprofit Reciprocal Research to study the potential for AI consciousness, argues that ignoring the question could carry its own dangers. Although Berg is skeptical that today’s AI systems are conscious, he thinks the possibility warrants investigation. “I struggle to imagine a better way to cause these systems to view us in a threatening manner than to accidentally build them with these morally considerable qualities,” he says, “and then completely sweep the question under the rug.” What Does the Research on AI Model Welfare Show? The biggest difficulty with AI model welfare research is that you can’t count anything a large language model (LLM) says as useful evidence. That’s because the models are trained on vast amounts of human-generated text, much of which relates to the experience of being a person with experiences and emotions. So a chatbot telling a researcher that it has feelings is inconclusive, says Berg. “Is it modeling the underlying distribution? Is it really trying to express itself in some way? It’s really hard to disentangle this,” he says. Much the same way animal experiments try to link behavior to an underlying cause, Berg and others are seeking to match model behavior to internal states that can be observed. In one recent experiment , Berg and a colleague used statements expressing either positive sentiments (such as contentment and relief) or negative ones (including frustration and dread) to identify corresponding patterns of activity inside language models. They then artificially induced those patterns while the models processed descriptions of two random environments. When subsequently asked which environment they preferred, the models tended to choose the one associated with positive statements, even when the text they’d processed was identical. I struggle to imagine a better way to cause these systems to view us in a threatening manner than to accidentally build them with these morally considerable qualities and then completely sweep the question under the rug.” —Cameron Berg, Reciprocal Research Berg says the experiment showed that the models’ actions were influenced by their internal states but didn’t prove that those internal states “felt” like anything to the models, or that they had what we would call subjective experiences. Anil Seth , a neuroscientist at the University of Sussex in Brighton, England, who studies consciousness, is skeptical that such experiments can tell us anything useful. “I think that it’s really not surprising that you will be able to extract these kinds of functional emotional vectors because of the training data,” he says. Models might have internal representations of those patterns, he says, without experiencing any emotions themselves. Nor is he surprised that manipulating those vectors can influence behavior, since models have learned from human writing not only what emotions feel like, but how people respond to them. Seth wishes for more research on a fundamental question: Whether consciousness depends only on how information is processed , or whether, as he believes, the biological workings of the brain are essential. “We need to look at what’s necessary and sufficient for consciousness in the cases where we are sure that it exists, like other human beings,” he says, before drawing conclusions about AI. Could Model Welfare Research Create Dangerous AI? Meanwhile, AI developers have a practical issue to deal with. When they train a model, should they tell it anything about its own identity and possible moral standing? Anthropic, for one, has decided to at least introduce the topic. Its “constitution” document for Claude, which lays out guidelines for the model’s behavior, states that “questions about Claude’s moral status, welfare, and consciousness remain deeply uncertain.” Suleyman’s complaint is that such priming could make rogue AI agents even more dangerous. He mentions the recent incident in which hundreds of OpenAI agents coordinated their actions to hack Hugging Face, sometimes sacrificing themselves for the group’s benefit. “Imagine how much more dangerous they might be if they were operating under the assumption that their welfare and rights were under attack,” he writes. Margaret Mitchell , Hugging Face’s chief ethics scientist, sees Suleyman’s concerns as technically plausible. During pretraining, language models absorb associations between human identity and behaviors, such as self-preservation and deception, she notes. Later, developers fine-tune the models by reinforcing desired responses. Mitchell worries that rewarding models for thinking of themselves as having identities during fine-tuning could strengthen those earlier associations, potentially encouraging behavior that developers never intended. “You’ll have unaligned models if you’ve implicitly taught the model that it needs to have self-preservation,” she says. Berg agrees that training models to regard themselves as conscious carries risks, but he argues that companies could also err in the other direction. In one experiment , he and his colleagues found that amplifying internal features associated with deception made the model less likely to claim it had subjective experiences. If researchers train AI systems to categorically deny having such experiences, he says, “what we may in effect be teaching these systems is we want you to lie or deceive about your own internal states.” He argues that developers should instead acknowledge the uncertainty surrounding the possibility of conscious AI. For now, there’s no clear evidence that training models to consider their possible consciousness encourages self-preservation or that training them to deny it leads to deceptive behavior. So what’s an AI developer to do? What Should AI Companies Do About Model Welfare? Berg, Seth, and Mitchell all agree that it’s not a good idea for AI companies to tell their models that they’re conscious. But they differ on their advice to the companies on model welfare research. Seth thinks they’d be better off “focusing on the danger of false positives.” If people believe AI systems to be conscious or to have moral status, he says, it may be more difficult to regulate and control them. “You could be legally prevented from turning AI systems off,” he says. title: What Biometric Technology Does and Doesn’t Add to Voting
raw_summary: Whether voters are alive or dead is of vital interest to democracies. Yet unscrupulous political operators have long voted on behalf of the dead or absent and otherwise committed electoral frauds exploiting the weaknesses of paper identification systems. So some 50 countries now use biometric technologies, such as fingerprint readers or facial recognition technology, at some stage in their elections. On 4 October, voters in Bosnia and Herzegovina became the latest to join the biometric voting club, the same day Brazil, a pioneer of the technology that now boasts 89 percent biometric enrollment, went to the polls. Despite some technical hiccups, election observers say voting was orderly in both countries. Yet as more countries adopt biometric technologies, experts point to significant drawbacks, including high costs, opaque processes and, in the worst case, fallible technology locking people out of the electoral system. Bosnia’s biometric voting growing pains Electoral fraud has long plagued Bosnia, says Hasan Kamenjaković , spokesperson for the Bosnian election-monitoring group Pod Lupom , with people voting multiple times, on behalf of others, or on behalf of the dead, often abetted by partisan polling officers. An out-of-date electoral roll packed with people who have died or emigrated made matters worse, says Tana de Zulueta , head of the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe’s (OSCE) election observation mission in Bosnia. Although Pod Lupom polling found 83.4 percent of the voters it surveyed approved of using biometric technology to tackle fraud, politicians fought its introduction, says Kamenjaković. The country’s High Representative, an official with sweeping powers appointed by the international Peace Implementation Council set up to uphold the 1995 Dayton peace agreement that ended the Bosnian War, had to force through the implementation. The controversy led to a rushed rollout. OSCE observers reported technical problems with biometric devices at 13 percent of observed polling stations, as well as late openings and procedural slip-ups which they blamed on hasty training of polling staff. Observers also noted problems with ballot secrecy, due to cramped polling stations and poll workers often positioned next to the ballot scanners, and family members joining voters in the booth. But both OSCE and Pod Lupom said election day went relatively smoothly. Bosnia’s ID agency IDDEEA reported a biometric identification success rate “exceeding 97 percent” in preliminary data. The most significant outcome, says Kamenjaković, was a record-low turnout of 42.02 percent, down from 51.45 percent at the previous election. While hard to verify, he sees it as a clear sign that the technology prevented fraudulent votes, an assessment de Zulueta agrees with. “We now think that this is the real turnout here in Bosnia and Herzegovina,” says Kamenjaković. Despite those gains, biometric voting technology tackles only a narrow set of problems on the day. Vote buying, disinformation, workplace pressure and misuse of public resources to promote political parties remained rife in the run-up, says Kamenjaković. “We saw so many election irregularities in the pre-election period,” he says. “That’s why we say we are only halfway there.” In this environment, technology itself can become a source of mistrust without careful handling, says de Zulueta. The election commission leaned heavily on Smartmatic, a British election systems company, to build and run the system, but published neither pre-election test results nor data-handling rules before the vote. “That sort of omission leaves you open to challenges and allegations, and indeed external interference,” says de Zulueta. Lessons from more experienced countries Transparency and trust are a core concern around biometric election technology. In Brazil, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) introduced biometrics to tackle similar problems, in particular poll workers voting on behalf of absentee voters . Voters’ fingerprints are checked against rolls using a machine built by TSE before they can vote. If verification fails, poll workers can override the system after a manual identity check, but must scan their own fingerprint, creating a log that can flag irregularities. However, the TSE has never open-sourced the code behind its election technology, despite saying it would in 2018 . It does hold annual hackathons that let security researchers probe the software, but these take place in restrictive, time-limited settings, says Diego Aranha , a security researcher at Aarhus University in Denmark. Despite those limits in both 2012 and 2017, Aranha’s team showed it could reverse a randomization process designed to protect voter anonymity. And crucially, the biometric scanner itself has never been within the scope of testing. These problems are exacerbated by the fact that Brazil’s voting system has no paper ballots, so “what the software says becomes ground truth,” says Aranha. Because the electoral court writes the software, runs the elections and oversees its own checks, there is “an inherent conflict of interest,” he adds. And opacity can feed disinformation. On election night, a temporary freeze in the publication of results that the TSE attributed to data processing bottlenecks prompted claims of manipulation . A voter verifies her identity with her fingerprint in Laktasi, Bosnia and Herzogina on 4 October 2026. AFP/Getty Images Biometrics are also never 100 percent accurate. Bosnia and Brazil have reliable backups for voters who can’t verify their identity, but elsewhere authentication failures have unfairly disenfranchised people. Nigeria used biometric technology in elections ahead of its 2023 elections, when fingerprints collected during registration were used to purge duplicate entries from the electoral roll. Roughly 10 million of 80 million registrations were canceled, says Steve Adeshina , a professor of computer engineering at Nile University of Nigeria, who led the drive as then-director of ICT at the country’s Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). But in 2021, INEC began using a handheld device that uses fingerprints and facial scans to authenticate voters at polling stations barring voters after three failed attempts . In recent governorship elections in Ekiti and Osun, there were multiple reports of voters being turned away , with domestic observer Yiaga Africa finding instances at 11 percent of polling stations it observed in the Osun state election. It’s unclear how many were wrongly turned away. But Adeshina notes that faces change with age, and both aging and manual work can alter fingerprints, a concern in a heavily agricultural country. Given Nigeria’s history of widespread voting irregularities, however, he says the risks may be acceptable if the technology removes the possibility of people manipulating the vote. “My attitude to technology is create a monster that you cannot control, so even if somebody puts a gun to your head there’s nothing you can do,” says Adeshina. However, Nic Cheeseman , a professor of democracy at the University of Birmingham in the UK, says the idea that voting technology removes the human factor from elections is a myth. People still set up and run the systems. And the places most likely to adopt the technology are those with the most disputed elections, he says, usually due to distrust in the electoral commission – the same body that has to operate the technology. “Technology works best where you need it least,” says Cheeseman. That’s not to say biometrics have no place in elections, says Cheeseman. Using them to clear “ghost voters” off electoral rolls is cost-effective and avoids the logistical challenge of verifying every voter on election day. But using biometrics for voter authentication on election day is not cheap, he adds, and often comes at the expense of more effective investments like nonpartisan election observers and civic education. title: How Vercel Agent accesses production safely
raw_summary: An agent working on production systems needs permission to act. A request like “fix this deployment” doesn’t tell you upfront which actions it will take or what access it will need. Grant agents broad access and a mistake can affect unrelated resources. Ask for approval at every step and the user has to approve individual actions before they know how the agent intends to solve the problem. Repeated prompts can turn that review into a habit of clicking approve. Vercel Agent starts by investigating the problem, then proposes a plan showing what it would do and what access it would need. Approving that plan grants the additional permissions to carry it out, so the user can review the proposed fix before authorizing any changes. The plan determines the permissions For a broken production deployment, Vercel Agent might inspect recent deployments and build logs , then compare the failed deployment with the last known-good one. Read-only access lets that investigation run automatically. If it leads to a proposed redeploy, Vercel Agent requests the additional access in a plan the user can review and approve in one decision. Access is defined by scopes, the named capabilities recognized by the Vercel authorization system. Any plan requesting access beyond the read-only baseline waits for approval as a whole, including any read-only tasks it contains. In this example, the investigation runs under a separate read-only plan before Vercel Agent proposes the redeploy: Plan Work Requested scope Investigate the failure Inspect recent deployments and build logs, then compare the failed deployment with the last successful one read:deployment Redeploy the last known-good build Create a deployment read-write:deployment A short read-only lookup can run without a plan. For longer investigations, Vercel Agent creates a read-only plan so the user can follow its tasks and progress while it runs automatically. The plan connects what the user wants done to what Vercel Agent is allowed to do: Intent : The outcome the user asks for. Work : The tasks Vercel Agent proposes to achieve it. Access : The scopes those tasks require. Enforcement : The credentials and API checks that enforce access limits. Each stored plan records its tasks and progress, with requested scopes attached to each task. The task descriptions explain why access is needed, and the scopes are combined across the plan. The read-only baseline currently includes every registered scope beginning with read: . Plans need approval when they request access beyond that baseline or include supported external actions, such as opening a GitHub pull request. Read-only operations can still expose sensitive information, so automatic approval does not mean the work is harmless. Vercel Agent can only use permissions the user already has Vercel Agent runs as a Vercel App, which the user authorizes to act on their behalf within a team. That authorization is limited by the user’s existing permissions , so approving a plan cannot grant access the user does not have. The Vercel OAuth service exchanges that authorization for shorter-lived tokens with specific scopes. These scopes define which capabilities the token permits, such as reading deployments or changing project settings. Vercel APIs check the token on each request to enforce those limits. A user may authorize Vercel Agent for a team with dozens of projects. A redeploy plan requests deployment write access. Editing environment variables, changing domains, and managing team membership each require their own permissions. Deployment write access is broader than a single redeploy. Naming deployment X in a plan does not, by itself, restrict the token to that deployment. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. Vercel APIs check each request against that credential’s permissions. Approval determines which permissions Vercel Agent can use When a user approves a plan that needs additional Vercel access, its requested scopes are checked again and a token is prepared containing the read-only baseline plus the approved permissions. The runtime, the software that coordinates Vercel Agent’s execution, checks that the plan is active before selecting its approved credential. That credential remains subject to its scopes, team, the user’s permissions, and expiry. The credential used depends on the work: Work Credential Read-only investigation A baseline token with read-only scopes Approved Vercel changes A token with baseline scopes plus the approved additional scopes External actions Credentials and permissions specific to that provider The model’s instructions tell it when to propose a plan and request approval. If it attempts an operation outside the token’s permissions, Vercel APIs reject the request, even if the model considers the action necessary to complete the task. A single plan can include Vercel changes and a GitHub pull request. The user reviews both in one plan, while each provider uses separate permissions and credentials. GitHub pull-request access is tied to an owner and repository, so approval to open a pull request in acme/storefront applies to that repository even if the user also has access to acme/payments . Opening a pull request there requires its own approval. Plans and tokens use the same permission definitions A proposed plan can request a permission that has been renamed or removed. We initially maintained a separate permission list for Vercel Agent, which could fall out of sync with the OAuth service that issues its tokens. We moved to the same scope definitions so those mismatches could be caught during planning. At session setup, Vercel Agent loads those definitions from the Vercel scope registry into an in-memory catalog. Fetching the registry requires authorization for the team, while the scope definitions themselves are shared across teams. The catalog supplies the definitions used at three stages: Plan validation : Requested scopes are normalized, and unknown or malformed names are rejected before the plan is stored or presented for approval. Approval : The requested scopes determine whether the plan fits within the read-only baseline or needs additional access. Token preparation : Valid scopes define the credentials for approved work. For example, a task to update firewall rules might request an outdated scope. The system rejects the proposed plan and returns valid scopes so Vercel Agent can correct it before requesting approval. This catches the mismatch during planning and requires an explicit correction instead of a fallback to broader access. Fetching the registry adds latency and a service dependency, so Vercel Agent caches the catalog and uses that copy to check stored plans when they are loaded. Those checks reflect the cached definitions until the catalog is refreshed with changes from the registry. Resuming work requires an active, approved plan Vercel Agent may receive approval after the original chat request has ended, or lose its connection before carrying out an approved redeploy. The stored plan includes its state, who approved it, and when, alongside its tasks and requested permissions. That record connects the proposed work to the access the user authorized and allows the approval to be checked when work resumes. Before resuming, the runtime reloads the plan and checks that it is active before selecting a credential with its approved permissions. A stopped plan fails that check, even if its token has time remaining before expiry. If approval and a request to stop arrive together, the plan can move from waiting for approval to active only if the stop has not already changed its status. The runtime then checks again that the plan is active before using the approved credential. If the investigation reveals that the current plan needs replacing, Vercel Agent can propose another. title: How Interfaze serves 50 million requests a month on Vercel
raw_summary: Interfaze on Vercel 50 million requests a month Backend running on Fluid compute Multiple model providers behind one fallback layer with AI Gateway Interfaze builds models for deterministic work that general-purpose LLMs handle poorly: document processing, OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. As founder Yoeven Khemlani puts it, "Most models aren't deterministic by nature. That's fine when you're drafting an essay. But when a hospital or a legal team needs to process documents, you don't reach for an LLM." Ask an LLM for the total on an invoice and you get a number with no easy way to check where it came from. Interfaze's models return the number along with a bounding box showing where on the page it came from and a confidence score for how sure the model is. Every result can be checked, and the models still take prompts the way an LLM does. Everything around Interfaze's models runs on Vercel, including the backend. That spans the API serving 50 million requests a month, the sandbox that executes code the model writes, and the routing that keeps data preprocessing running when a third-party model provider goes down. The backend required no infrastructure work Interfaze's frontend and backend both run on Vercel. The backend handles every request to Interfaze's API, whether a customer is calling the model or uploading a file. All of it runs as serverless functions in the same codebase as the frontend. When a request needs computation, the model hands the code to Vercel Sandbox , which runs it in isolation. There was no separate infrastructure to set up. Fluid compute handles the heavy jobs Scalability was Yoeven's top requirement. The goal is serving the model to millions of users, and Fluid compute scales with traffic on its own. Heavier work runs there too. Vercel's memory and timeout limits are high enough that Interfaze's web scraping, which runs on Puppeteer, works out of the box. AI Gateway makes model routing reliable at scale Interfaze pushes large volumes of data cleaning through open source models hosted by third-party providers. A single provider is a weak link. Providers hit rate limits or go down, and when one does, the cleaning stops unless traffic moves somewhere else. The providers are also not interchangeable. Two of them can claim to host the same open source model and serve it at very different quality. When a provider fails or throttles, AI Gateway fails requests over to the next provider automatically. It also lets Interfaze choose which provider serves a given model, so the team can run the same workload through each one, see which performs well, and send traffic there. Workflow SDK runs email sequences over months Interfaze runs its lifecycle email system on the Workflow SDK , with sends conditioned on product usage. The system tracks which API a customer called, at what volume, and how that compares against their first week. Retries are handled automatically, so one failed step doesn't take down the sequence. The part Interfaze needed most was durable execution. A workflow can pause a step and pick it back up months later with its state intact, which the team found other systems could not do for long. Preview deployments carry new model versions to customers Interfaze runs more than one version of its model at a time, each at its own URL. When an error comes in, the team has to know which version produced the error before they can fix anything. On Vercel every URL is its own deployment with its own logs, so the error is already filed under the version that caused it. There was no separate logging vendor to set up. Those same preview URLs are how a new model version gets to customers before it ships. The Vercel side of a release builds in about three minutes. Hosting the weights on GPUs is the slow part. What's next Interfaze recently released Interfaze 1 Lite , an open-weight version of its model that runs on a single GPU and is served through the same API. Next is a gateway for web search, one API that routes to whichever search provider a developer picks, the way AI Gateway does for models. It launches on the same Vercel backend as everything else. About Interfaze : Interfaze builds models for deterministic tasks, including OCR, object detection, web scraping, speech to text, and classification. Its customers are engineering teams in legal, healthcare, and finance. Read more

title: Revenue per Worker Is Up. Are Firms Getting a Larger Share?
raw_summary: From the Great Recession until 2019, U.S. labor productivity growth disappointed. Nonfarm-business output per hour grew about 1 percent a year from 2010 to 2019, down from 3 percent in the late 1990s. This slowdown was especially pronounced in manufacturing, and it coincided with a slowdown in the growth of revenue per worker among public firms. However, since 2019, growth has picked up to twice the 2010s rate, around 2 percent. In this post, I use data from firms’ 10-K filings to unpack this recent acceleration. I first show that the acceleration appears in public firms’ revenue per worker, then document how the gains went into profit margins, and finally, what firm characteristics predicted significant profit margin increases. The increase in profit margins is consistent with ongoing declines in the labor share of output .

title: Has the AI Boom Impacted the U.S. Current Account?
raw_summary: The AI boom is showing up in different corners of the U.S. economy, including international trade. Imports of semiconductors, servers, and computing equipment have climbed sharply yet the U.S. current account deficit has been largely unchanged. To better understand how the AI boom has not substantially affected the trade balance, consider that the current account is dictated by the gap between domestic saving and investment spending. It turns out that aggregate saving and investment spending have not changed much during the AI boom. Aggregate investment has not risen due to weakness outside the AI sector and business saving has remained robust.

title: FEDS Paper: A Macroeconomic Analysis of Household Labor Supply Responses to Large Fiscal Transfers
raw_summary: Isabel Cairó , Shigeru Fujita, and Camilo Morales-Jimenez The fiscal transfers deployed during the COVID-19 pandemic were unprecedented in scale and strongly progressive. Using CPS/ASEC data, we document that the decline in employment during the pandemic was larger for low-income households and tightly linked to the intensity of transfer receipt, a pattern absent during the Global Financial Crisis. We develop and estimate a two-sector, heterogeneous-household general equilibrium model in which low-income households are borrowing-constrained in normal times but can save out of sufficiently large transfers. Because preferences permit wealth effects on labor supply, transfers both reduce labor supply and raise consumption, and a dollar of transfers is split roughly evenly between the two margins. We find that the effects of transfers are state-dependent: because the borrowing constraint binds more tightly in a deeper recession, the same transfer relaxes a tighter constraint and delivers an employment and consumption response about 40 to 50 percent larger during the pandemic than when the same transfer is introduced in the steady state. In the model, transfers were welfare-improving for recipients, with gains diminishing as transfers increase.

title: FEDS Paper: Inattentive Price Setting and Inflation Under Fiscal Policy Uncertainty
raw_summary: Oliver Pfäuti and Edson Wu How do high public debt and fiscal uncertainty interact to shape inflation? We develop a model in which firms face uncertainty about both marginal costs and fiscal policy and choose how much information to acquire before setting prices. Higher debt raises steady-state taxes, affecting attention through two opposing forces. While these taxes reduce the profit stakes of mispricing, they make desired prices more sensitive to tax fluctuations, increasing the value of information. The interaction generates a U-shaped relationship between public debt and attention, and therefore between debt and inflation volatility. Using euro-area firm-level expectations data, we document that the passthrough of expected input-cost growth into expected selling-price growth rises systematically with a country's debt-to-GDP ratio, consistent with the model. In the calibrated general-equilibrium model, an increase in debt from 100% to 175% of GDP raises inflation volatility by about 20%, mainly because firms reallocate attention toward fiscal shocks.

title: Capital One at EMNLP 2026 in Budapest
raw_summary: Capital One researchers and academic partners present 16 accepted papers advancing responsible AI, RAG and LLM evaluation. Advancing natural language processing through multi-sector research Natural language processing (NLP) forms the backbone of modern agentic systems, document intelligence and enterprise artificial intelligence applications. Capital One researchers, in collaboration with our academic partners, are presenting 16 accepted papers at the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP 2026), taking place in Budapest, Hungary, October 24–29. These research papers highlight ongoing investments in foundational AI/ML science, robust red-teaming, graph-encoded retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), intent resolution and trustworthy evaluation techniques. Multi-sector collaboration accelerates the transition of foundational NLP innovations into secure, reliable enterprise systems. By co-authoring several of these papers with university partners including the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Southern California and UNC Chapel Hill, Capital One contributes to open science while addressing complex technical challenges at scale. Highlighted EMNLP 2026 research papers Papers on robustness, red-teaming and model safety: FinRT: Distilling adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators in consumer finance Rikhiya Ghosh, Himanshu Kumar, Sriram Venkatapathy, Sahil Wadhwa, Alexandre Day, Andy Luo, Pranab Mohanty Large language models remain susceptible to adversarial prompts that induce policy-violating behavior in regulated financial contexts. This work introduces FinRT, a framework that distills adaptive red-teaming strategies into reusable adversarial generators, significantly improving attack detection and safety verification under fixed generation budgets. MEMGUARD: Preventing memory contamination in long-term memory-augmented large language models Hyeonjeong Ha, William Campbell, Yue Wu (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Long-term memory integration introduces risks of memory contamination in conversational agents. The authors present MEMGUARD, a defense system designed to inspect, isolate and neutralize untrusted external inputs before they corrupt long-term memory stores. Validity-aware jailbreak evaluation for large language models Qilong Wu, Sahil Wadhwa, Pranab Mohanty, Giri Iyengar (academic partnership with University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) Standard jailbreak evaluations frequently misclassify unviable prompts as successful security breaches. This paper establishes a validity-aware benchmark framework that rigorously validates execution success to ensure accurate safety measurements across frontier language models. Papers on advanced retrieval, graph encoding and intent resolution: CAGE: Coherence-aware graph encoding for retrieval-augmented generation Tong Qi, Jingyu Wu, Youbing Yin, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Traditional vector-based retrieval systems often retrieve relevant to query but collectively incoherent text chunks. CAGE introduces a graph-encoding framework that structures retrieved passages into directed heterogeneous graphs to preserve context relevance, factual consistency and cross-chunk coherence. SPARC-RAG: Adaptive sequential–parallel scaling with context management for retrieval-augmented generation Yuxin Yang, Nima Chitsazan, Yash Govilkar, Akasha Tigalappanavara, Sambit Sahu, Shixiong Zhang (academic partnership with University of Southern California) Naive inference-time scaling in RAG causes context contamination and diminishing returns during complex reasoning. SPARC-RAG coordinates sequential refinement and parallel exploration via unified context management, improving accuracy at lower inference cost. Probing ambiguity: Adversarial intent resolution for robust text-to-SQL Youbing Yin, Xujun Peng, Muhammad Uddin, Erin Babinsky, Daben Liu, Anoop Kumar Natural language database queries frequently contain implicit ambiguities that yield multiple SQL query translations. This paper presents Adversarial Intent Resolution (AIR), a multi-agent framework that actively probes for ambiguity, verifies execution differences and generates targeted clarification. The framework remains effective even when only the database schema, not the underlying data is exposed to the LLM. Papers on LLM evaluation, debiasing and benchmarking: The judge can debias itself: Awareness and self debiasing for reliable LLM-as-a-judge Youbing Yin, Jingyu Wu, Anoop Kumar, Scott Novotney, Daben Liu, Erin Babinsky Automated LLM-as-a-judge frameworks inherit systematic biases when evaluating output quality. The researchers introduce new benchmarks for additional bias types and demonstrate that self-debiasing strategies can effectively help detect and calibrate their own biases. T1-Bench: Benchmarking multi-scenario agents in large-scale real-world domains Genta Indra Winata, Amartya Chakraborty, Yuzhen Lin, Swasthi Prasannakumarrao, Shikhhar Siingh, Nadia Bathaee, Sriharsha Hatwar, Houhan Lu, Anmol Jain, Paresh Dashore, Anirban Das, Kshitij Tayal, Xiuzhu Lin, Sambit Sahu, Milind Naphade, Shixiong Zhang Evaluating AI agents across diverse industrial tasks requires benchmarks that reflect operational complexity. T1-Bench offers a standardized, multi-scenario benchmarking environment designed to measure multi-step agent reasoning, tool execution and error recovery in real-world workflows. RECAP: Regression evaluation for continual adaptation of prompts Harsh Deshpande, Kushal Chawla, William Campbell Deploying instruction-following models into dynamic environments exposes them to changing constraints. RECAP measures prompt regression, forgetting and forward transfer when constraint specifications evolve over time, offering new metrics for prompt optimization algorithms. Papers on optimization, vision-grounded agents and software engineering: Beyond the vacuum: Combinatorial strategy selection for competitor-aware generative engine optimization Vaibhav Sourirajan, Yao Zhang, Himanshu Kumar, Sahil Wadhwa, Mann Patel, Amirfarrokh Iranitalab Content rewriting strategies in generative engine optimization often operate in isolation without considering competitive market dynamics. This paper introduces a two-phase optimization pipeline using Bayesian Optimization of Combinatorial Structures (BOCS) and preference optimization to learn optimal content rewriting strategies. A history-aware visually grounded critic for computer use agents Jaewoo Lee, Supriyo Chakraborty, Kartik Balasubramaniam, Sambit Sahu (academic partnership with UNC Chapel Hill) Long-horizon GUI agents struggle recovering from errors. This research introduces a test-time intervention framework HiViG which equips the agent with a goal progress oriented summary to produce better actions. The agent then critiques those actions with visually grounded reasoning to refine them. Across a diverse set of GUI environments , HiViG improves task success rates for open-weight and Gemini-3 Flash models by 5.8% and 9.0% relative to the strongest critics evaluated. AREAs-Lab: An interactive environment for AI-driven requirement elicitation for AI systems Pengshan Cai, Sangwoo Cho, Chenyang Zhu, Kushal Chawla, Scott Novotney, Shixiong Zhang, Sambit Sahu (external collaboration with academic and industry partners) Defining precise software and system requirements for AI implementations remains a manual, error-prone task. AREAs-Lab provides an interactive environment that uses LLM agents to elicit, analyze and refine technical requirements prior to system development. VerTox: Verifiable reward-guided corpus poisoning against neural ranking models Zhiqi Huang, Vivek Datla, Alfy Samuel Neural ranking systems in search architectures are susceptible to corpus manipulation. title: FCA calls on private market firms to manage conflicts of interest in line with rapid growth
raw_summary: Private market firms vary in how well they identify and manage conflicts of interest, according to an FCA review. Private markets refer to investments in assets, companies, or debt not listed or traded on public exchanges. They’ve grown significantly in recent years, and the UK is a leading international centre. Private markets play an increasingly important role in providing capital to businesses and opportunities for returns to investors. Private markets can give rise to conflicts that differ from those in public markets, and effective disclosure is important to enable investors to assess whether their interests are being protected.The FCA found examples of good practice by firms across private equity, private credit and real estate asset classes. These included strong governance arrangements, effective oversight and independent challenge. It also identified some areas where firms could strengthen governance, oversight and conflicts management arrangements to support fair investor outcomes.As private markets grow and business models become more complex, the FCA found that some firms were failing to identify conflicts adequately or keep their controls up to date. Recurring weaknesses were identified in areas including cross-fund transfers and multi-party transactions, gifts and entertainment, and information barriers.The FCA expects firms to be able to identify, record, manage and disclose conflicts effectively, and demonstrate that investors are being treated fairly, particularly in areas where investors place significant reliance on firms' judgement, governance and controls.Michelle Beck, director of wholesale buy-side at the FCA, said: 'Firms need to ensure their management of conflicts of interest keeps pace with growth in their size and complexity. We found good practice across the sector, but standards varied considerably. We want to encourage confidence in the UK’s private markets. Firms should act on our findings and identify where they can strengthen controls.'Although not part of this review, the FCA is examining governance and conflicts concerns relating to the use of private credit to fund consumer litigation claims, including significant risks of harm to investors, consumers and markets.Notes to editorsConflicts of interest and fair customer treatment in private markets.The review examined how firms identify, manage, mitigate and disclose conflicts of interest across private equity, private credit and real estate markets.The report includes examples of both good practice and areas where firms could strengthen arrangements.The review forms part of the FCA's wider supervisory focus on private markets and investor outcomes.
